title: The Last Run of the Number 7 Bus
paragraphs: At 9:40 on the last night of June, the number 7 bus left the square for the final time. The route had run for 38 years between the town and the railway station, 14 kilometres each way. The bus company said too few people used it.

The last bus carried 47 passengers, more than it had carried on any night that year. Some brought flowers, and one man played a small radio. The driver, Mr Kwok, had driven the route for 19 years. He stopped at every stop even when nobody was waiting.

A woman gave him a paper bag of oranges, and he put it beside his seat. Mr Kwok said: "I know every hole in this road. I know which corner floods and which tree drops fruit on the roof. A new driver will learn it, but it will take him a year."

The company lost about 900,000 yuan on the route last year. A minibus now runs four times a day, but it does not go to the station. It stops at the top of the hill, and passengers must walk down 180 steps to reach the trains. That walk takes eleven minutes.

The town asked for the route to be kept for another year and was refused. In July, 600 people signed a paper asking for a bus that goes to the station. The company said it would study the idea in December. Mr Kwok now drives the number 12.

title: The Bicycle Shop That Closed on a Sunday
paragraphs: On the last Sunday in October, a bicycle shop on a corner in Liwan closed its door for the last time. It had opened in 1993, and the same family had repaired bikes there for 33 years. The sign above the door was painted by hand.

The shop was small, about 18 square metres. It held 200 tools and a wall of spare parts in small wooden boxes. The owner, Mr Sung, 61, said the rent had gone from 900 yuan a month to 7,200 in twelve years.

In its last month, the shop repaired 74 bikes. Most were children's bikes with flat tyres or loose chains. Mr Sung charged 15 yuan for a repair and often took nothing from students. He said he could not raise the price because the people who came were his neighbours.

One girl came back three times with the same puncture, free each time. Mr Sung said: "People do not repair bikes now. They buy a new one for 400 yuan and leave the old one outside. I am not angry about it. I am just tired of paying for a shop that holds broken things."

On the last day, 30 people came to say goodbye, and someone brought a cake. Mr Sung gave his tools to two young men who fix bikes in the park on Sundays. The shop will become a phone repair counter. The hand-painted sign now hangs above his kitchen door.

title: Nine Hundred Trucks of Silt
paragraphs: For 30 years, the pond in a small park north of the market smelled of old water in summer. In March, workers began to remove the mud at the bottom. The job took 74 days and filled 900 trucks.

The pond is only 40 metres across but 2.1 metres deep in mud. The mud was carried to a field outside the town and left to dry. Workers also took out 11 bicycles, 4 shopping carts, and a metal gate that nobody could explain. The oldest thing found was a coin from 1963.

The work cost 1.7 million yuan, paid by the town and a group of shop owners. Not everyone agreed with the plan. A residents' group wanted the two old trees at the south end kept, and the first plan had them removed to make the bank straight.

The town changed the plan after 240 people signed a letter. The trees stayed, and the bank now curves around them. A low stone wall was built along the north side. New water came in from the canal in May, and 300 small fish were put in during June.

A woman who has lived beside the pond since 1988 said: "I stopped opening my window in July. This year I opened it and smelled nothing. I stood there for a while to be sure." The park added six benches, and the town will test the water every month for a year.

title: The Lane With Two Names
paragraphs: In May, a lane in the old part of town got a new name. The town office changed Market Lane to Old Market Lane, because there is now a second Market Lane near the new hall. The vote was 7 to 4.

The change cost 4,800 yuan for 18 new signs, and it took workers two days to fix them. Two sign makers worked from a small truck. The post office printed 2,000 notices for residents. But 63 people signed a paper asking for the old name to stay.

Mr Lau, 72, who has run a tea shop in the lane for 41 years, said: "My address is on 400 paper bags. My customers have written it on their hands. Now the town tells me the lane is called something else, and I must pay to print again."

The town office said the new name was needed for ambulances and delivery drivers. In April, a food delivery rider spent 25 minutes looking for number 14 because two lanes had the same name. The office also offered to reprint the first 100 bags for each shop, and it answered 90 calls that week.

In the end, both sides got part of what they wanted. The signs now say Old Market Lane in large letters and Market Lane in small ones below. Mr Lau has not changed his paper bags. He says people still find him, and that is what a name is for.

title: The Cinema With Sixty-Four Seats
paragraphs: A cinema that closed in 2017 opened again on the first Saturday of September, but it no longer shows films every night. The town bought the building for 3.2 million yuan and turned it into a community hall with 64 seats.

The seats are the same red seats from 1994, cleaned and repaired by 22 volunteers. The screen is new, and the old projector sits in a corner under a cloth. The first event was a night of old photos, and 130 people came, so 66 of them stood at the back.

The repair was not easy. Rain had come through the roof for years, and the ceiling above row four had to be rebuilt. The town was 80,000 yuan short in June, and a local business paid for the sound system instead.

Some residents wanted the building to be a shop, because the town has no large supermarket. A survey in July found that 58 percent wanted a hall, 21 percent wanted a shop, and the rest did not care. The town will decide on the fourth evening in December.

Ms Chan, who sold tickets there as a student in 1996, said: "I stood in the same place on Saturday and my hands remembered the ticket machine. The machine is gone, but the room still sounds the same when people talk." The hall will open four evenings a week.

title: The Crossing That Took Four Years
paragraphs: On March 3, a pedestrian light began working at a junction in the west of the town, four years after residents first asked for one. The junction has two schools, a clinic, and no bridge within 600 metres. About 900 students use it every school day.

The first request went to the town in 2022. It was refused because the road was too narrow for a light and a turning lane. Residents collected 3,100 signatures in 2024. In November 2025, a boy on a bicycle was hit by a car and broke his arm. He now walks with his mother.

The light cost 260,000 yuan, and workers moved a bus stop 40 metres to make room. In the first week, the town counted 2,400 people crossing each day. Most of them are children. The wait for a green light is 48 seconds.

A shop owner on the corner said: "Forty-eight seconds is long when it rains. But I have watched children wait for it, and they wait. Before, they ran." She has counted them from her window. The shop has been in her family for 30 years.

Not everyone is happy. Drivers say the light adds three minutes to their morning trip, and one delivery company wrote a letter of complaint. The town will count traffic again in September. For now the light stays on from six in the morning until eleven at night.

title: The Public Tap on Corner Street
paragraphs: For 40 years, a public tap at the end of Corner Street gave free water to anyone with a bottle. The tap was put there in 1986 by a shop owner who is now 91. On February 9, the water stopped.
A pipe under the road had broken, and the town turned off the tap while it was repaired. The repair was expected to take ten days. It took 47, because workers found a second leak under the pavement.

During that time, 30 families carried water from a tap at the clinic, 200 metres away. Ms Yip, 68, who fills two bottles every morning, said: "I have a tap at home. I come here because I meet people. For seven weeks the corner was empty, and the street felt like a different street."

She brings a small folding chair too. The town first said the tap would not come back, because the water was not tested and the pipe was in the way of a new drain. Ms Yip wrote to the town office twice.
After 180 people signed a letter, the town changed its mind. It put in a new pipe with a filter and a metal button. The work took four days and cost 12,000 yuan. Most of the money went on the filter.

The tap returned on April 2 with a small sign: drinking water, tested monthly. It runs for eight seconds when pressed. Ms Yip says eight seconds is enough for one bottle, and she now brings a second one for a neighbour.

title: The Week Every Door Got a Number
paragraphs: In July, every door in twelve lanes of the old town received a new number. The town said the old numbers were confusing, because some lanes had two number 8s and one lane had no number 13 at all. In total, 1,100 doors were renumbered.

The work took nine days. Two workers painted the numbers in black on small white plates and fixed them beside each door. Each plate cost 11 yuan. The town also printed a small map for each lane and put it at the entrance.

The change caused trouble at first. In the first two weeks, the post office returned 46 letters because the addresses did not match. A noodle shop received three boxes meant for a laundry. The town put one person on a phone line for address questions for a month.

A postman who has walked these lanes for 16 years said: "I knew every door by the colour of its paint. Now I read the plates, and I am slower. In a year I will be faster than before, but this year I am not." He keeps the old map in his bag.

Most residents accepted the change. One woman, 84, kept her old number on a piece of paper beside the new plate, because her family in another city had used it for 50 years. The town said it would not remove the paper. The new numbers will appear on maps in October.

title: The Pool That Opens at Half Past Six
paragraphs: On a Tuesday in March, a middle school in Zengcheng opened its swimming pool at half past six in the morning. Forty-two students from grade 7 and grade 8 stood by the water in the cold air, some of them in shorts, waiting for the teacher to blow the whistle.

The pool was built twelve years ago but had been closed since 2023, when the water heater failed. A new heater cost about sixty thousand yuan. The school could not pay for it alone, so the parent committee raised half the money in six weeks, mostly in gifts of two hundred yuan.

The first morning did not go well. The water was nineteen degrees, and after eight minutes three students climbed out with blue lips. A coach named Mr Qiu stopped the class and sent everyone to the showers. "Cold water is not training," he told the group. "It is just cold."

The school moved the class to half past six in April, when the sun warms the water earlier. It also bought a cover that keeps heat in at night. That cost another nine thousand yuan, and the committee had to ask parents a second time. Eleven families said no.

By May the water reached twenty-six degrees, and sixty students were coming three mornings a week. Mr Qiu still checks the gauge before every class. He keeps the numbers in a notebook, one line for each morning, and he says the pool will close again in November, when the mornings turn cold.

title: One Table Under the Banyan Tree
paragraphs: For nine years, students at a middle school in Liwan played table tennis on one concrete table under a banyan tree. The table had no net, only a row of broken bricks, and the tree dropped small fruit on it every June.

In April a grade 8 class measured the table and found it was two metres long, not two point seven four. Someone had cut it short to fit between two roots. A student named He suggested building a new one in the open yard, where there was space for two tables.

The workshop teacher, Mr Tan, gave them a wooden board and four metal legs but no money for a net. The class raised eighty yuan by selling old books, and bought two nets and six balls. The rest of the money went on paint.

Building the tables took three Saturdays. The first board warped after rain because nobody had painted the underside. They turned it over, painted both sides, and waited two days. "We learned more from the second board than the first," Mr Tan said.

The new tables opened in May. About thirty students now play at lunch, and the old concrete table stayed where it was, under the tree. The class put a small sign on it: short table, long history. The fruit still falls on it every June, and someone still wipes the top before a game.

title: The Rope That Broke at Two Hundred
paragraphs: On a Friday afternoon in October, a jump rope team at a middle school in Panyu was trying to break its own record of one hundred and ninety skips in a minute. At skip two hundred, the long rope snapped in the middle.

The team had twelve members and one rope. They had used it for two years, and the centre had worn thin and grey. A replacement cost one hundred and twenty yuan, and the school said the money would take two weeks to arrive.

In the meantime, the team borrowed a rope from a primary school next door. It was four metres shorter, so two members had to stand closer, and the rope hit the ground too early. Their count fell to one hundred and sixty.

The coach, Ms Feng, did not change the training plan. She made the team practise with the short rope for eight days and write down each mistake. The notes showed that most misses came from the two students at the ends, who had to turn faster than the others.

The new rope arrived on a Wednesday. On the first try the team reached one hundred and ninety-eight, two short of the record. They tried again on Saturday and got two hundred and four. Ms Feng said the eight days with the wrong rope had taught them more than a new rope ever could.

title: Ten Centimetres Too Low
paragraphs: In September, a grade 7 student at a middle school in Haizhu brought a tape measure to the basketball court. She wanted to know if the hoop was the right height. It was not. The rim stood at two metres and ninety-five centimetres, ten centimetres below the standard.

Nobody knew how long it had been wrong. The court was built in 2016, and the poles had been set in concrete. A worker said the base may have sunk after heavy rain, or the wrong pole may have been ordered.

Fixing it was not simple. The pole could not be raised, so the school had to buy two new rims with longer arms, at four hundred yuan each. That took three weeks, and during that time the court had only one working hoop.

Some players liked the low rim. Three students said they could dunk for the first time, and one asked if the school could keep it. The PE teacher, Mr Xu, said no. "A low hoop makes you feel good for a week," he said. "Then you play on a real court and miss everything."

The new rims went up in October. The student who measured the hoop now carries the tape measure in her bag and has checked the volleyball net, the long jump board, and the height of the classroom door. All three were correct, which she said was a little disappointing.

textbook_series: 自编新闻练习材料（配合课堂打字训练，不绑定教材版本）
title: The Warm-Up Nobody Wanted
paragraphs: Last year, the nurse at a middle school in Baiyun treated twenty-six sprained ankles in one term. Most of them happened in the first ten minutes of PE class, before students had run or stretched.

A new PE teacher, Ms Gao, looked at the nurse's record and found a clear pattern. Fifteen of the injuries were in grade 7 classes that had PE right after a long maths lesson. Students ran straight from their desks to the court.

In March she added an eight-minute warm-up: two laps of walking, then slow jumps, then ankle circles. Students complained that it wasted time. One class started a petition to skip it, and forty students signed it in one lunch break.

Ms Gao did not cancel the warm-up, but she cut it to six minutes and let the class choose the music. One song was too fast, so they chose again. In the second term the nurse treated nine sprained ankles, down from twenty-six. Two of the nine came at lunch, not in class.

The petition is still on the classroom wall, with the signatures and a note added in June in three pens: we still think it is boring, but we are used to it. Ms Gao says that is fair. She keeps the note next to the nurse's numbers and shows both to new classes in September.

title: A Pitch on the Roof
paragraphs: In April, a middle school in Tianhe opened a small football pitch on the roof of its canteen. The pitch is thirty metres long and eighteen metres wide, with a fence three metres high and a net above it.

The school had no flat ground left. The main field was used for morning exercises, and the back yard was a car park. The roof was strong enough, an engineer said, but only if the pitch was light: no concrete, no grass, and a surface of rubber tiles.

The tiles cost about one hundred and twenty thousand yuan. The school paid half, and a local sports group paid the rest in return for using the pitch on Sunday mornings. The net has a small hole where the ball goes through, and nobody has mended it yet.

The first problem came from the neighbours. A family in the building next door wrote to the school about the noise of balls hitting the fence. The school moved practice to before six in the evening and added a second layer of netting, which cost eight thousand yuan.

About ninety students now use the roof each week. On windy days the ball flies over the net, and someone has to run down three floors to fetch it. A grade 8 boy said he has fetched the same ball eleven times this term, and the number is written on the wall by the stairs.

title: Twenty-Two Students Walk to School
paragraphs: Every morning at ten past seven, twenty-two students meet at a small park in Huangpu and walk to school together. The walk is one point four kilometres and takes about twenty minutes. Two parents walk at the front and the back.

The group started in February, when a mother named Ms Luo counted eleven cars waiting outside the school gate each morning, most of them carrying one child from the same street. She wrote the number on a card and put it on her fridge.

The school agreed to the plan but asked for rules. Students had to wear bright vests, cross only at the marked crossing, and stay in pairs. One corner has no pavement, so the group crosses the road twice to stay safe. The vests cost fifteen yuan each, and the parents paid for them.

Rain was the first test. On a wet morning in March only six students came, and two turned back halfway. The group now checks the forecast the night before and cancels the walk if the rain is heavy. On light rain days they go, with umbrellas.

By June the group had grown from twenty-two to thirty-one, and the number of cars at the gate had fallen to four. Ms Luo says the walk is slower than driving and that her son sometimes arrives with wet shoes. She says he also arrives awake, which is not something she could say before.

title: Less Salt in the Soup
paragraphs: In March, the canteen at a middle school in Yuexiu cut the salt in its soup by one third. The cooks did not tell students. They simply put less salt in the pot and waited to see what the students would say.

The first week was bad. Students left about forty litres of soup uneaten each day, compared with twelve before. A grade 7 class wrote a letter to the canteen: the soup tastes like hot water. A teacher read it twice and agreed with the class.

The manager, Mr Pang, met the class and explained the reason. The school nurse had found that many students ate salted snacks at break, so the canteen lowered the salt in cooked food to balance it. She weighed a bowl of the old soup: two point one grams, against one point four now.

The class suggested a compromise: keep the salt low but add other things for taste, such as tomato, dried shrimp, and a little ginger. The cooks tried three versions in one week and asked two hundred students to vote.

The winning version used tomato and ginger and half the old amount of salt. By May, uneaten soup had fallen to eighteen litres a day. Mr Pang says it is still above that, and he doubts it will ever go back. The class's letter is now on the canteen wall, next to the menu.

title: The Wall With Three Colours
paragraphs: In October, the gym of a middle school in Zengcheng got a climbing wall. It is four metres high and six metres wide, and it is covered with holds in three colours: yellow for easy, blue for medium, and red for hard.

The wall was built by a company from another city and took nine days, including two days of rain. The school had wanted a taller wall, but the ceiling was too low, and the engineer said four metres was the safe limit without a rope system.
Safety rules came before the first climb. Students must have a teacher within two metres, must not pass the yellow line at three metres, and must land on the mats, which are thirty centimetres thick.

In the second week a grade 8 boy fell from the top yellow hold and hurt his wrist. He was not badly hurt, but the school closed the wall for four days and added a rule: no climbing in the last ten minutes of a class, when students are tired.

About forty students climb each week, and nine come on Wednesday afternoons to set new routes. Their routes are marked, and anyone can try them. Holds are brushed every Friday, because chalk makes them slippery. The boy with the hurt wrist came back in November. He started on yellow and has not tried red yet.

title: Lights Out at Ten
paragraphs: For six weeks this spring, a middle school in Baiyun asked its grade 7 dormitory to turn off the lights at ten o'clock. Before that, lights could stay on until half past ten, and many students read or did homework under a desk lamp after the main switch went off.

The change came from a survey of two hundred and forty students. Only sixty said they slept eight hours on school nights. Most said they slept six or seven, and thirty-one said they often felt sleepy in the first class.

Not everyone agreed. Some parents said their children needed the extra time for homework. A father wrote to the school that his daughter's maths scores would fall. The school answered that homework should end by nine, and asked teachers to check.

The dormitory staff now walk the corridor at ten and knock on doors where light shows under the door. In the first two weeks they knocked on about twenty doors a night. By the fifth week the number was three.

The school has not measured scores yet, but it has measured sleep. A second survey in May found that one hundred and forty students now sleep eight hours or more. The father who wrote the letter said his daughter's maths score stayed the same, and she stopped falling asleep at breakfast.

title: The Bell That Rang Four Seconds Late
paragraphs: On a Monday in March, students at a middle school in Liwan noticed that the bell rang four seconds late. The first bell, at ten past eight, came at fourteen seconds past. By lunch it was six seconds late, and the teacher in room 302 had already written the time on the board.

The bell system was twenty years old. It used a small clock in the office that sent a signal through a wire to a speaker on each floor. The clock had a tiny motor, and the motor had worn down after millions of turns.

Two grade 8 students in the science club asked if they could study it. Their teacher, Mr Xia, gave them a stopwatch and a notebook. For five days they timed every bell, wrote the number in a table, and found the delay grew by about one second a day.

The school could replace the system for eleven thousand yuan. Instead, Mr Xia showed the students how to open the clock and clean the motor with a soft brush. It took an hour, and the delay fell to less than one second. A new system is planned for next year.

The fix lasted until June, when the motor began to slow again. The students now clean it every eight weeks and keep the table on the wall. Mr Xia said he will miss the old clock, and the students will miss being the only people in school who knew why the bell was late.

title: Four Hundred Sticks and a Box of Glue
paragraphs: In April, a science club at a middle school in Panyu built a bridge out of four hundred ice cream sticks. The bridge was one metre long and twenty centimetres wide, and it was held together with white glue. The club wanted it to hold thirty kilograms.

The design came from a picture in a book. The first bridge, made of two hundred sticks, broke at twelve kilograms. It failed in the middle, where two sticks met end to end and touched on only a small area.

The club changed the design. They overlapped the sticks by three centimetres, added a second layer on the bottom, and let each layer dry for a full day. Drying took longer than building, and the club met on four Saturdays instead of two.

The second bridge held nineteen kilograms, then cracked with a sound like a small door closing. A student named Wei said the failure was useful. "We know where it is weak now," she said. "The middle is still the middle."

The final bridge held thirty-four kilograms for eleven seconds before the middle gave way. The club did not try again, because only six sticks were left. The bridge is now on a shelf in the science room, with a photo of the broken middle and a card that lists the three weights: twelve, nineteen, thirty-four.

title: The Printer That Ate a Spool
paragraphs: In February, a middle school in Tianhe bought a small 3D printer for its design class. It cost four thousand yuan and came with one spool of plastic, enough for about three hundred small objects the size of a key ring.
The first big print was a model of the school gate. It was eleven centimetres tall and took nine hours. At hour seven, the printer stopped. The plastic had wound around the spool and jammed the feed.

The teacher, Ms Ren, and three students spent two hours taking the printer apart. They found a small piece of plastic stuck in the tube. The tube was thinner than the plastic, so one small bend was enough to stop it. The model was ruined, and half a spool was wasted.

The class changed its rules. Every print over three hours must be checked at the end of each lesson. The spool must be wound by hand before a long print, and the printer must sit on a flat table, not on a desk that someone leans on.

The second gate model finished in ten hours and came out in one piece, though one tower leaned two millimetres. It stands in the school office. Ms Ren says the printer has taught the class something the textbook could not: a machine does exactly what you tell it, including the mistakes.

title: A Panel on the Canteen Roof
paragraphs: In March, six solar panels went up on the roof of the canteen at a middle school in Haizhu. Each panel is one and a half metres long and weighs nineteen kilograms, and together they cover about nine square metres of the flat roof.

The panels cost fourteen thousand yuan, paid by a fund from the district. The school expected them to make about six kilowatt hours a day, enough to run the canteen lights and two fans for an afternoon on a sunny day.

The first full month was a disappointment. The panels made only three point eight kilowatt hours a day. A worker found that a water tank cast a shadow on two panels from eleven in the morning until two in the afternoon.

Moving the panels was not possible, because the tank could not be moved. Instead, the school added two more panels on the other side of the roof, where there is no shadow. That cost another four thousand yuan and raised the daily output to five point one in full sun.

A monitor shows the number each day, and students write it on a board. On a cloudy day in May the number fell to one point two, and a grade 7 class asked why. The science teacher took them up, showed them the tank and its shadow, and said: this is why we measure.

title: The Drone That Counted Trees
paragraphs: In April, a geography club at a middle school in Zengcheng used a drone to count the trees in a small park near the school. The park is about two hectares, and nobody knew how many trees it had. The park office guessed eight hundred.

The drone flew for eighteen minutes at a height of forty metres and took two hundred and six photos. A student named Fang then spent three evenings joining the photos into one large picture on a school computer.

Counting was harder than flying. The club first counted one thousand and forty trees, then found they had counted several trees twice where photos overlapped. The second count gave nine hundred and twelve. It took two more evenings.

Permission was the slow part. The club needed a teacher to fly the drone, a parent to watch, and a letter from the park office. The letter took three weeks, and the first two flight days were too windy to fly.

The final map shows nine hundred and twelve trees, with the ten largest marked in red. The map hangs in the school corridor for a week before it goes to the park office. The office has asked for a copy and plans to use it when it plants new trees in autumn.
Fang says the number will be wrong by next year, because trees grow and some are cut. She wants to fly again in autumn. "A map is a photo of a Tuesday," she said. "It is not the park."

title: Sand, Charcoal and a Plastic Bottle
paragraphs: In May, a science class at a middle school in Baiyun built a water filter from a plastic bottle, sand, small stones, and charcoal. The class wanted to turn muddy water from a fish pond into water clear enough to see through.

The first filter was a bottle cut in half, turned upside down, and filled in layers: cloth, charcoal, sand, stones. Water went in at the top and came out brown at the bottom. It took four minutes for one litre.

The class tested the water by looking through it at a black cross on paper. Before filtering, the cross could not be seen at all. After the first filter, it was faint but visible. The water looked like weak tea.
The teacher, Mr Kong, was careful with the result. He said clear water is not safe water, and the class must never drink what comes out. The point was to learn how layers work, not to make a drink.

The second filter used finer sand and a longer cloth layer. It produced clearer water in two minutes, but the flow stopped after twenty litres because the sand packed tight. The charcoal came from the kitchen, and the class rinsed it five times before use, because the first rinse water was black.
The class decided that a filter is a trade: clearer water, slower water. The bottles are now on a shelf, with the muddy jar beside them, where anyone can see the two colours side by side.

title: The Rocket That Went Sideways
paragraphs: On a windy Thursday in April, a grade 8 class at a middle school in Huangpu launched water rockets on the school field. Each rocket was a plastic bottle with a paper cone, filled with one third water and pumped by a bicycle pump.

The class had calculated that a rocket with seven hundred millilitres of water and a pressure of three bars would fly about forty metres. The first rocket went eleven metres, then turned and hit the fence.
The problem was the home-made fins. They were made of cardboard and glued on by hand, and one fin was two millimetres thicker than the others. At speed, the rocket turned toward the heavy side.

The class rebuilt the fins with a paper template and weighed each one on a small scale. The fins were the only part they could change without new bottles. The second rocket flew thirty-four metres in a straight line and landed on the grass. The third went forty-one metres and was lost over the wall.

The teacher, Ms Du, stopped the launch after the fourth rocket because the wind pushed them toward the road. The class wrote one rule for next time: no launch in wind above three metres per second. The lost rocket is still on the other side of the wall, and nobody has asked for it.

title: A Radio That Reached Thirty Kilometres
paragraphs: In March, two students at a middle school in Conghua set up a small radio in the science room and talked to a school in another town thirty kilometres away. The signal was weak and full of noise, but the words came through.

The radio belonged to the physics teacher, Mr Liao, who had used it when he was a student. It needed an antenna, and the best place was the roof of the teaching building, five floors up. The antenna was a piece of wire eight metres long, tied to a metal pole with rope.

Getting to the roof took two weeks of letters. The school worried about lightning and about students climbing the ladder. In the end a worker fixed the antenna, and students were allowed up only with Mr Liao and only in dry weather.
The first try failed. The antenna was too low, and a metal water tank blocked the signal to the north. They moved it two metres to the side, and the other school came through at half past four.

The two schools now talk for twenty minutes every Wednesday. The conversations are short and mostly about weather and homework. Mr Liao says that is enough. "A radio is not a telephone," he said. "You have to wait, and you have to listen, because only one person can talk at a time."

title: The Bike That Charged a Phone
paragraphs: In May, a student at a middle school in Yuexiu built a stand that turns an old bicycle into a phone charger. The back wheel spins a small motor, and the motor sends power through a wire to a USB socket.

The parts came from three places: a broken bike from the school store room, a motor from an old toy car, and a socket from a shop that repairs computers. The stand has a wooden frame and two clamps that hold the phone still. The whole stand cost about sixty yuan.

The first test was slow. Pedalling for ten minutes added only four percent to the phone. The student, a grade 8 boy named Guo, found that the motor turned too slowly at normal speed and lost power in the wire.

He changed to a smaller wheel, which made the motor spin faster, and shortened the wire by half a metre. Ten minutes then gave eleven percent. He also added a small board that keeps the power steady, because the phone stopped charging when he pedalled slower.

The stand sits in the science room and is used at break. Guo says it is not a charger, because a full charge would take more than an hour of hard pedalling. He says that is the lesson: "Energy is easy to use and hard to make. I did not believe that before I tried."

title: The Lift That Stopped at Floor Three
paragraphs: On a Tuesday morning in April, the lift at a middle school in Tianhe stopped between the second and third floors with four students inside. It did not fall. It simply stopped, and the doors would not open.

The students pressed the alarm button and waited. A worker arrived in nine minutes, opened the doors with a key, and helped them climb out one by one. Nobody was hurt, but one student said she would take the stairs for a month.

The lift was eleven years old. A repair company found that a small sensor near the third floor had come loose and was sending a wrong signal. The sensor cost forty yuan, and the visit cost six hundred.

The school closed the lift for five days and asked the company to check every floor. Two more sensors were loose. The company also found that the alarm bell had been disconnected for a year, and nobody had noticed.

The lift reopened with a new rule: no more than six people, and a teacher must ride with grade 7 classes. The company now visits every six months instead of once a year. A small sign now hangs inside, with the date of the last check written in pen.
The student who took the stairs for a month still does, though the lift works. She says the stairs are slower, and she is never late because of them. Her friends now wait for her at the bottom.

title: The Lantern Maker Who Ran Out of Paper
paragraphs: For three weeks before the Mid-Autumn Festival, Mr Liang made paper lanterns in a workshop in a lane in Yuexiu. This year the neighbourhood committee ordered six hundred lanterns, twice the usual number, because two more streets had joined the celebration and wanted the same kind.

The order arrived in mid-August, later than usual. Mr Liang and his two helpers cut bamboo strips in the morning and glued red paper at night. A simple lantern took about twenty minutes. Six hundred lanterns meant two hundred hours of work, and they had nineteen days.

On the twelfth day the paper ran out. 'I counted the sheets three times,' Mr Liang said. 'There was enough for four hundred and ten lanterns and not one more.' The supplier in Foshan said the paper would take a week to arrive, five days too late.

He did not wait. A printer two streets away sold him three hundred sheets of thicker paper at almost double the price. The colour came out a little darker. The committee agreed to pay the extra four hundred yuan, but only after an argument about whether every lantern had to look the same.

In the end the first four hundred and ten lanterns were pale red, the last one hundred and ninety deep red. They hung in two groups, the darker ones on the east side. On the festival night a woman stopped under them and said they looked as if they had hung there for years.

title: A Lion Dance Team With Eleven Dancers
paragraphs: On the second day of the Spring Festival, a lion dance team in a village in Huadu had eleven dancers and three lions. A full team is eighteen: six people under the lions and twelve on drums, gongs and cymbals. Four had gone to the city for work and three were ill.

The team leader, Mr Tang, did not cancel the visits. He moved two drummers under the lions and taught a fourteen-year-old boy to hold the cymbal. The boy had watched for two years but had never played in front of people. In the first hour he missed the beat four times.

'A lion with three legs still walks,' Mr Tang said. 'It is slower, and it cannot climb the high platform, but the door visits must be done.' The team walked to twenty-six houses that morning instead of the usual forty. At each door the dance was cut from six minutes to four.

The shorter route cost the team money. Each house usually gives a red packet of thirty to fifty yuan, and the team keeps half of it for new drum skins and travel. This year the total was about eleven hundred yuan, five hundred less than last year, and new skins must wait until summer.

At the last house, an old woman asked for the full dance anyway. The team did a short version on the flat ground and left out the platform. She clapped for a long time. Mr Tang said practice will start in November next year, so nobody has to learn the cymbal on the first morning.

title: The Flower Market That Opened at Five
paragraphs: The flower market on a street in Liwan opened at five in the morning this year, three hours earlier than before. The reason was simple: the street is narrow, and by eight the trucks could no longer get in with more flowers.

Two hundred and six stalls stood along nine hundred metres of road. The first trucks arrived at half past four with peach branches, kumquat trees and gladiolus. Workers carried the trees by hand for the last hundred metres, because a truck cannot turn at the corner near the old temple.

Not everyone was pleased. People living above the market complained about the five o'clock noise. The street office held a meeting with eleven residents and nine stallholders. The stallholders agreed to stop using loudspeakers before seven, and the residents agreed not to call the police about boxes being unloaded.

'We did not win and they did not win,' said Ms Weng, who has sold gladiolus at that corner for nineteen years. 'We just moved the loud part to the afternoon, when nobody is asleep.' She opened at five every morning and closed at eleven at night.

By the first evening it had sold about forty thousand branches, the street office said. On the last night the stalls were still open at two, and the road was covered with leaves and string. Six cleaners and two trucks took until five to clear it. Next year the market will open at four.

textbook_series: 自编新闻练习材料（配合课堂打字训练，不绑定教材版本）
title: The Stage That Moved Under the Trees
paragraphs: A village opera stage in Panyu was moved forty metres on the morning of the festival, after rain filled the open square where it stood. The stage had been built over four days by eleven men, and the first performance was due at ten.

The opera group arrived at nine with six singers and nine musicians. Water stood ankle deep in places on the square. The village head, Mr Pan, walked around it twice, looked at the sky, and then pointed at the row of banyan trees beside the school wall.

Moving the stage took three hours and thirty men. The boards were taken apart in sections, carried under the trees and rebuilt. Two boards broke on the way. The new place was smaller: seats dropped from four hundred to two hundred and sixty, and the front row where older people usually sat was lost.

'We started ninety minutes late and I thought half the village would go home,' Mr Pan said. 'But they stood at the back, in the wet, and waited.' The first act was cut by twenty minutes so that the last one could finish before dark.

About three hundred and forty people watched in the end. The village paid the full price of four thousand yuan and added two hundred for the broken boards. In the spring, Mr Pan said, the square will get a stone edge and a drain, so the next stage will not have to move.

textbook_series: 自编新闻练习材料（配合课堂打字训练，不绑定教材版本）
title: The Drum That Cracked in the Second Race
paragraphs: At the second race of the dragon boat festival in Zengcheng, the drum on one boat cracked. The boat carried forty-two paddlers, one steerer and one drummer, and it was leading by half a boat length when the sound suddenly changed.

The drummer, a young man named Guo, hit the skin harder because he thought he had made a mistake. The crack grew longer. Within twenty seconds the drum made no sound at all, and the paddlers, who row by the beat, began to pull at different times.

A boat without a drum cannot keep time. The team finished fourth, eleven seconds behind the winner. On the bank, an old boat builder looked at the drum and said the skin had been wet for two days and had then dried too fast in the sun, which made it hard and easy to split.

'Nobody trains for a silent drum,' Guo said. 'For a moment I just watched the paddles and tried to count in my head.' He counted to forty, but the boat had already turned a little sideways, and the steerer had to work hard to bring it back.

A new skin costs six hundred yuan and takes eight days to fit. The team borrowed a drum from a village across the river and came third in the last race, enough for a place in the county competition. Guo now covers the drum whenever the boat leaves the water.

title: Three Thousand Rice Dumplings Before Dawn
paragraphs: Twelve women in a lane in Haizhu made three thousand rice dumplings in two days before the Dragon Boat Festival. The dumplings went to nine old people's homes and to a free table at the entrance of the lane, where anyone could take two.

The work started at six on the first morning. Each dumpling needs four bamboo leaves, about ninety grams of rice and a filling of pork or beans. A fast pair of hands can wrap forty in an hour. The oldest woman in the group, Ms Cai, is seventy-one and wrapped sixty in the first hour.

On the second afternoon they ran out of bamboo leaves. The market had sold out two days earlier. A shop in Fangcun had four thousand leaves left, but the price had gone up from eight yuan to eleven yuan for a bundle of five hundred, and the shop would not go lower.

'We argued for ten minutes about whether to buy,' Ms Cai said. 'Then someone said the dumplings are not for us, so we bought.' The extra cost was ninety yuan, paid from a box that usually holds about six hundred and is meant for the festival meal.

The dumplings were boiled in four large pots from ten at night until three in the morning. Two hundred and forty went to the old people's homes, and the rest were given away at the table. By nine the next morning only eleven were left, kept for the women who had done the wrapping.

title: The Dragon That Needed Sixty Carriers
paragraphs: A paper dragon sixty-eight metres long was carried through the streets of a village in Baiyun on the fifteenth day of the first month. It needed sixty carriers, and two days before the parade the village had found only forty-eight.

The dragon is made over five weeks by a workshop that has built it every year for thirty years. The head alone weighs nineteen kilograms. The body is sixty-four paper rings on bamboo hoops, and each ring needs one person to hold it up and keep it straight.

The village asked the middle school for help. Sixteen students in grade 8 agreed to carry the last rings, where the dragon is lightest. They practised for two evenings in the playground, walking in a line and turning at the corners, while an older man shouted the count from a chair.

'The tail is the hardest place for a beginner,' said Mr Xu, who has carried the head for eleven years. 'You cannot see the person in front of you, and you have to feel the pull. If you turn too early, the whole body folds.'

The parade took ninety minutes for two kilometres. Two paper rings were torn by tree branches, and a woman on a balcony repaired them with tape as the dragon waited. The village spent about four thousand yuan on paper and paint, three hundred more than last year. The students have asked to carry the tail.

title: The Bus That Left at Four
paragraphs: On Qingming morning the first bus to the cemetery in Conghua left at four o'clock, an hour earlier than last year. Sixty-two people were waiting in the dark outside the village office, some with flowers and some with a small bag of food.

The village rents three buses every year. The road to the cemetery is single and narrow, and after seven it fills with cars from the city. Two years ago a bus took two hours to travel eleven kilometres, and the older people on it did not reach the graves until almost ten.

This year the first bus carried fifty-one people and arrived at twenty past four. The second left at half past four and the third at five. The village paid one thousand two hundred yuan for the three buses, the same as last year, because the company kept the old price.

Not everyone wanted to leave so early. Several older people said the graves should be swept after sunrise, not before. The village head, Ms Deng, said the early bus was for people who had to work at eight, and that anyone who preferred a later hour could take the seven o'clock bus.

'My mother is eighty-three and she still came at four,' Ms Deng said. 'She said the dead do not mind the hour, but the living have to be home for lunch.' By six the road was full of parked cars, and the three buses were already on their second trip up the hill.

title: The Couplets Written on the Pavement
paragraphs: For eleven days before the Spring Festival, Mr Feng wrote couplets on the pavement outside a market in Tianhe. He wrote about two hundred pairs, some sold for ten yuan and some given away to people who said they had no money that week.

He works with a brush, a bottle of ink and a roll of red paper. A short pair takes about four minutes, a long one eight. He sits on a low stool, a stone on the paper to hold it down, and works without a table because the paper is longer than any he owns.

This year the cold came early. On the third morning the ink turned thick and the brush left dry lines in the middle of a word. He put the bottle inside his coat and warmed it with his hands, but he still lost about twenty minutes and had to write three pairs again.

A market guard also asked him to move twice, because the stall stood in front of a fire door. Mr Feng moved four metres to the left, where there was less foot traffic. He sold eleven pairs that day instead of the usual thirty, and one of the eleven was bought by the guard.

'A machine prints a hundred an hour,' he said. 'But people stop to watch the hand. That is what they pay for, and why I am slow.' On the last evening he counted one thousand seven hundred and forty yuan, two hundred less than last year. The cold, not the guard, was why, he said.

title: The Ancestor Hall With a New Roof
paragraphs: The ancestor hall in a village in Huadu closed for four months and reopened on the festival's first day with a new roof. The old roof had leaked for nine years, and buckets stood in the side room every spring.

The hall was built in 1911 and is used for weddings, meetings and the festival meal. Water had damaged two beams and a painting above the door. A builder said the roof needed six hundred tiles, forty new beams and about ninety thousand yuan, and half the work had to be done before the rains.

Money was not the hard part. The village raised it in three months from one hundred and forty families, with one gift of ten thousand yuan. The argument was about the door. Three older families wanted the old door repaired; others wanted a new one, because it was too low for tables at festivals.

In the end they kept the old door and cut nothing. Instead, tables are now carried in through a side opening that was once a window. 'We spent two meetings on that window,' said Mr Huang, who kept the accounts. 'The roof took eleven minutes.'

The reopening began at eleven with a lion dance and a meal for three hundred and ten. The accounts were on a board by the door: ninety-two thousand four hundred yuan spent, four thousand one hundred left. The rest pays for a light above the door, so the old wood shows at night.

title: The Field With Three Roads Around It
paragraphs: A vegetable field of about two mu in a village near Huadu now has a road on three sides. The farmer, Mr Liao, has refused to sell it for four years, while the fields around it became buildings, a car park and a row of small shops.

The roads came one by one. The first was built in 2019, the second in 2022 and the third last spring. Each time, workers offered a price for the land. Each time he said no, and the road was built around him, which cost the road company about forty thousand yuan more.

The field is thirty-one metres wide and forty-three long, small for a machine but enough for two people with hand tools. Mr Liao grows lettuce, spring onion and Chinese cabbage. He sells about sixty kilograms a week at a stall two kilometres away, and the walk takes him forty minutes.

The roads brought dust and, at night, light from a lamp four metres from his shed. He says the lettuce near the lamp grows faster and is ready a week early, which sounds good until the following week, when there is nothing left to cut and nothing to sell.

Asked why he does not sell, he said: 'The money would last five years. The soil has lasted my whole life.' His son works in a factory in Foshan and comes back on Sundays to help with the watering. The field will stay a field, Mr Liao says, until his arms stop working.

title: The Bus That Leaves at Six Forty
paragraphs: The village bus to the town leaves at six forty in the morning and comes back at five twenty. For eleven years it was the only public transport for four villages, and last October the company said it would stop the route before winter.

The route is twenty-three kilometres and carries, on average, nineteen people a trip. The company said a bus needs at least thirty passengers to cover fuel and the driver, and that the road's two low bridges also wear out the tyres faster than city roads.

The village office asked for three months. A survey counted passengers for two weeks: most were students going to the town middle school and older people going to market. The village offered to pay the company eight hundred yuan a month from a small fund, and forty families agreed to add ten yuan each.

'We did the numbers on the back of a newspaper,' said Ms Ouyang, who runs the village shop and kept the count. 'Nineteen people times four yuan is seventy-six a trip. It was never going to be enough, and we knew it.'

The bus still runs, but twice a day instead of four times. In the morning it is full; at noon it is often empty. The driver, Mr Lu, now waits ten minutes at the school gate so students do not have to run. The village will review the payment in June, before the new term.

title: Three Years to Get Eleven Streetlights
paragraphs: Eleven streetlights were switched on in a lane in Baiyun on a Friday evening in March. The lane is three hundred and forty metres long, and residents there had asked for lights for three years.

The first request was sent in 2023 and signed by sixty-two residents. The answer was that the lane belongs to the village, not the district, and the village said it had no money that year. The second request, a year later, came back with a price: about twenty-eight thousand yuan for lights, poles and cable.

Then came the argument about who pays for the electricity. The lane has forty-one households. Some wanted the cost split equally; others said the four shops at the entrance use the lane most and should pay more. Two meetings ended without a decision, and one ended with people walking out before the tea.

The shops finally agreed to pay a third, and the households paid the rest, about three yuan a month each. A retired electrician in the lane, Mr Tan, checked the old cable for free and found two places where it would have failed within a year, which added six hundred yuan to the bill.

'For three years we walked with phones in our hands,' said Ms Xia, who signed the first request. 'Now the children can see the steps.' The lights go off at eleven thirty. One resident has asked for midnight, and the village says it will decide after the summer, when the bill is known.

title: The Well in the Middle of the New Road
paragraphs: A stone well that stood in the middle of a village road in Panyu for more than a hundred years was moved fourteen metres last month, so that trucks could pass. The road was widened from four metres to seven, and the well sat exactly where the new edge would be.

The village had two choices: cover the well or move it. Covering was cheaper, about three thousand yuan for concrete and a metal lid. Moving cost nineteen thousand, most of it for a new base and for carrying the stones by hand.

Eleven men worked for six days. They took out the stone rings one by one, numbered them with chalk and rebuilt the well on a concrete base beside the road. The water came back after two days. Four families still use it for washing vegetables, and one shop uses it for its floor.

Not everyone agreed with spending the money. At the village meeting nine voted to cover the well and keep the nineteen thousand for the road. Seventeen voted to move it. One man said the well had been there before any of them and should not be filled with concrete to save a week.

'My grandmother carried water from this well,' said Mr Su, who watched from a chair. 'I did not want to tell my son it was under a truck.' The road opened in June. The well now has a low wall, and the village plans a sign with the year it was built, which nobody knows.

title: The Night Market That Stops at Ten
paragraphs: A night market on a street in Haizhu now closes at ten o'clock. Before this spring it ran until one in the morning, and the change came after eleven months of complaints from people living above the shops.

The market has one hundred and eighty stalls on six hundred metres of pavement. Most sell food, clothes and phone cases. About two thousand people pass through on a weekend night, and the street earns money that the district does not want to lose, which is why the first answer was no change at all.

The street office counted the complaints: two hundred and forty in eleven months, most about noise after midnight and rubbish left on the pavement. It then held three meetings with stallholders, residents and the cleaning company, and the second meeting lasted four hours.

The agreement has four parts. The market closes at ten. Loudspeakers are not allowed at any hour. Each stall pays two yuan a night for cleaning. And the stalls on the north side, nearest the flats, close at nine thirty, which affects thirty-one stalls.

'I lost about a fifth of my sales the first month,' said Mr Mai, who sells fried noodles. 'Then the people here started coming down to eat, because they could sleep.' The street office will count the rubbish again in September. It wants under forty bags a night; in April there were sixty-one.

title: Nine Students in One Minibus
paragraphs: Nine students from three villages now travel fourteen kilometres to a town middle school in a minibus that leaves at six twenty-five. The school was rebuilt in 2023, and the two small village schools closed in the same year.

The minibus is not a school bus. It belongs to a driver, Mr Wen, who also carries vegetables in the afternoon. The back seats were changed to fit nine students, and the village pays him nine hundred yuan a month, which is less than a bus company asked for the same route.

The road is narrow for the last three kilometres and has no streetlights. In winter the students leave in the dark and come back in the dark. In January the minibus was late seven times because of fog, and on two of those days the students missed the first class.

'I count them at every stop,' Mr Wen said. 'Nine in the morning, nine in the afternoon. If I have eight, I turn around.' He keeps a list on the dashboard with the name of each student and the village they come from, and calls the school if a student is not at the stop.

The arrangement costs the village ten thousand eight hundred yuan a year, less than a school bus but more than the old walk. Two parents have asked for a second vehicle so students in sports clubs can stay later. The village will look at the numbers in the autumn, when the new road is finished.

title: A Garden on the Roof of the Market
paragraphs: Sixty vegetable boxes were placed on the roof of a market in Yuexiu in April. The roof is flat and about four hundred square metres, and the boxes take up less than a third of it, leaving space for the water tank and the walkway.

The idea came from a shopkeeper, Ms Qiu, who grows spring onion in buckets behind her stall. She asked the market manager for the roof and was told that the building is thirty years old and the roof can hold only a certain weight, especially after rain.

An engineer said the roof could take about two tons in that area. Wet soil weighs much more than dry soil, so the first plan for ninety boxes was cut to sixty, and the boxes were made of light plastic instead of wood. The cost was seven thousand two hundred yuan, paid by eighteen shopkeepers.

Not all of them were happy. Three shopkeepers said the money would be better spent on a new drain at the front, which floods when it rains and sends water into the first two stalls. The manager agreed to fix the drain as well, but with market money, not garden money.

'The first month was terrible,' Ms Qiu said. 'The soil dried out twice and the wind took the tops off the beans.' They now water at six and have put a low net around the boxes. In July the garden gave forty kilograms of vegetables; the drain was finished in June.

title: The Car Park That Kept Half a Field
paragraphs: A plan to build a car park for one hundred and twenty cars on a field at the edge of a village in Zengcheng was cut in half last month, after residents collected eight hundred signatures in nine days.

The field is about six mu and is used for the village football game, the festival meal and, in winter, for drying rice. The village office said the cars from the new houses had nowhere to park and the lanes were blocked every evening, and that two ambulances had been stuck there last year.

The first plan took all six mu and put a hard surface over the whole field. Residents asked what would happen to the football game. The office answered that a small court could be built on the roof of the car park, which would have cost another four hundred thousand yuan, so it was dropped.

At the village meeting the vote was close: sixty-one for the full car park and fifty-eight for half. The head of the village, Mr Yao, then proposed a third plan, with sixty cars on three mu and three mu left as a field with a new drain and a better gate.

'The field is not just grass,' said Mr Yao. 'It is where the village meets.' The work ran from May to August. The car park fills by seven. The other three mu still hold the football game, and the October festival meal will use both halves, with cars moved to the school for a night.

title: The Man Who Delivers to Three Villages
paragraphs: Mr Kuang delivers parcels to three villages from a shop in a town in Conghua. He makes about one hundred and thirty deliveries a day on an electric tricycle that can carry sixty parcels at a time, and he knows every door without looking at the number.

The shop is the last pickup point before the hills. Before it opened, people had to collect parcels at the town office, eleven kilometres away, and the office closed at five, which meant half a day lost for anyone who went. Mr Kuang opened in 2021 and charges one yuan a parcel.

A small bridge stands on the road to the third village. It has a weight limit of one and a half tons, and the loaded tricycle comes close before a festival. Twice last year Mr Kuang left half the parcels at the bridge and went back for them, losing about an hour each time.

'The bridge is older than my father,' he said. 'I do not argue with it.' He now takes the hill road in the morning and the bridge road in the afternoon, when the load is lighter and the light is better for the narrow corner.

The work pays about three thousand yuan a month after fuel, and a new battery every two years costs one thousand six hundred yuan. Before the Spring Festival he carried two hundred and ten parcels a day and finished at ten. His wife now answers the phone so he does not have to stop.

title: Forty-Two Bags From One River
paragraphs: Forty-two bags of rubbish were pulled from a two-kilometre stretch of river in a village in Huadu on a Sunday in May. Most of it was plastic bottles, food boxes and pieces of fishing net, and two bags were only bottle caps.

The work was organised by a group of twenty-six volunteers from the city, who came by bus at seven in the morning. They had planned for sixty people, but the bus company changed the time twice and some people could not come, so each person had to carry more than planned.

The river is shallow in May, and volunteers could walk in it with boots. Four of them used long poles with hooks, and the rest filled bags on the bank and tied them in pairs. A farmer lent a small tractor to carry the bags to the road, which saved about an hour.

A few villagers were not pleased. One said the volunteers would not come back, and the rubbish would return in a month. Another said the real problem was the two pipes that run into the river above the village, and that picking up bottles was like drying a floor with the tap on.

'They are right about the pipes,' said Ms Hua, who led the group. 'We take out what we see. We cannot fix what we cannot reach.' The group has promised to return in September. The village has asked the district to look at the pipes, and a letter with forty-one signatures was sent in June.

textbook_series: 自编新闻练习材料（配合课堂打字训练，不绑定教材版本）
title: Three Days Under the Bridge
paragraphs: In early March, a television crew in Guangzhou spent three days under a bridge in Nansha. They were waiting for one cargo ship to pass. The plan was a single shot: a ship sliding under the bridge while a train crossed above it. The shot would last nine seconds.

The crew had a tide table and a ship timetable, but the two did not agree. The ship was late twice. On the first night, four people slept in a van for four hours with forty kilograms of camera gear beside them. Nobody complained, because the water was quiet and the radio was off.

Mr Mai, the cameraman, said, 'We did not need a better camera. We needed the ship to come at the right hour. For three days it came at the wrong one.' He checked the light meter every twenty minutes and wrote the numbers in a small book.

The best chance came at 4:40 on the second morning. The sky was still black, so the crew paid 1,800 yuan to hire two lights. The ship passed on time, but the shot showed only a grey shape and one white rail. The lights were too far away. The crew watched it twice and said nothing.

On the third morning, at 6:12, the ship came again with the sun behind it. That shot lasted nine seconds in a twenty-four minute film, and it is the one people remember. Mr Mai kept the failed night footage too, because the sound of the water was better.

title: The Number in the Margin
paragraphs: On a Tuesday in April, a newspaper in Foshan stopped its first edition before dawn. The front page said that a school reading room had served students for forty years. A fact-checker had found that the room opened in 2012, which made it fourteen years old.

The checker, Ms Qiu, found the date in three places. A photo caption said 1979, and a school history page said 1986. An old ledger said the room was built with money given in 2012, and the first book was stamped that September. She wrote the three dates on one page and drew a line under each.

Ms Qiu said, 'The headline was not a lie about the school. It was a lie about a number, and a wrong number is still wrong. Nobody had checked it because everyone liked the sound of forty years. It sounded like a long time, and it was not.'

The editor argued for an hour. He said forty years was a way of speaking, and the story was about books, not dates. Ms Qiu said the paper could not print a number it knew was false. Eight thousand copies were already on a truck outside, and the driver was waiting for a paper to sign.

The truck came back. The page was remade with a new headline and a short note at the bottom. The reprint of three thousand copies cost 4,600 yuan. Two readers wrote to the office to say they had never seen a correction on page one before.

title: The Door That Stayed Closed
paragraphs: In June, a bus driver in Foshan stopped a food cart that rolled down a slope toward a crowd. The cart was carrying about two hundred kilograms of vegetables. Nobody was hurt. A television crew wanted to interview him on camera and went to his flat three times in one week, once in the rain.

The first two visits ended at the door. The third ended with a note handed out through a gap. The driver, Mr Feng, wrote that he was sixty-one, that his wife was ill, and that he did not want his face on television for one small thing. Then he closed the door again.

Mr Feng said later, 'I told them I would talk on the phone and nothing more. I am not a hero. I stopped a cart because it was coming at me. Anyone with two hands would have done the same, and most people would have run. My neighbours know what I did, and that is enough for me.'

The producer wanted to keep asking. The reporter, Ms Deng, refused and said the man had said no twice. The channel lost the interview, and the film had no face for its main scene. The argument between them lasted two days.

The piece ran for four minutes and twenty seconds. It used a photo of the empty slope, forty seconds of the driver's voice, and no name. Mr Feng listened once and asked the station to take out his street name too. They did. The piece was watched about twelve thousand times that week.
source_title: 打字登山·自编新闻练习文 v1

textbook_series: 自编新闻练习材料（配合课堂打字训练，不绑定教材版本）
title: The Photo With the Wrong Year
paragraphs: A documentary about a river ferry in Zhaoqing used a black and white photo marked 1979. Two weeks before broadcast, a viewer called the station. He said the photo was from 1986, and he knew because he was the boy standing at the front of the boat. The film was almost finished, and the music had been recorded.

The researcher, Mr Tan, checked four details. The bus behind the ferry had a plate from a later year. A shop sign used a style of character that changed in the eighties. The boy's bag had a plastic strap, which came later. He put the four details on a board. The caption was wrong.

Mr Tan said, 'A photo is not a fact until you know where it came from. This one came from a box with no list. Someone wrote 1979 on the back in pencil, and for eleven years nobody asked who wrote it or why.'

Re-cutting cost two days and about 3,000 yuan. The narrator was on another job and could not record, so the new words appeared as text on the screen. The director first wanted to drop the photo and use a map of the river instead.

The photo stayed, with the right year. The viewer came to the office with his own copy of the same picture, taken by his uncle. The station scanned it and put both versions side by side at the end of the film, with one line of explanation. The two copies are not the same size.

textbook_series: 自编新闻练习材料（配合课堂打字训练，不绑定教材版本）
title: Ninety Seconds Without Sound
paragraphs: At noon on 12 May, a station in Zhaoqing went live from the opening of a small footbridge. Ninety seconds into the report, the sound stopped. At home, about forty thousand viewers saw a reporter's mouth move and heard nothing but a low hum.

The cause was found in four minutes. A cleaner had moved a chair, and one leg pressed a cable against the floor. The cable ran under a rubber mat that nobody had lifted for a month. The engineer, Mr Bao, saw a red light and ran the length of the bridge.

Mr Bao said, 'I had two choices. I could cut the live report, or I could put a phone against the microphone and hope. I chose the phone. It sounded like a man talking from inside a box, but people could hear the words. I had about four seconds to decide.'

The reporter repeated three questions, and the guest, an old bridge builder, answered each one twice because he could not hear the studio. The report ran four minutes over its slot and pushed the weather to the end of the programme.

The station logged thirty-one calls that afternoon. Most were complaints, but six said the phone sound was clearer than the usual live audio. Nobody in the newsroom laughed. The callers were right about one thing: the phone picked up the wind better. The next week, every cable in the van was taped to the floor with yellow tape.

textbook_series: 自编新闻练习材料（配合课堂打字训练，不绑定教材版本）
title: A Line in the Mud
paragraphs: On 3 November, a crew filming a wetland in Jiangmen sent a small drone up at 7:20 in the morning. The river was low. On the screen, a straight line ran across the mud for four hundred metres. It was too straight to be a path. The crew had come for birds, not shapes in the mud.

The director, Ms Luo, thought it was an old road. The boatman said it was a wall, and he had worked on this river for thirty years. They argued for two days and then took a boat out at low tide. The mud was soft, and the boat could not get closer than thirty metres to the line.

Ms Luo said, 'From the air everything looks like a plan. On the ground it looked like a row of stones with grass in the gaps. That was the moment the film changed. We stopped looking at the river and started looking at what people built beside it.'

Getting permission took six days. The wetland office first said no, because the mud was a resting place for birds. A retired worker, Mr Wei, came with them and said the wall was built in 1971 to hold the soil after a bad flood.

The line appears for twelve seconds in the thirty-minute film. It is not called a wall on screen, only 'a line built by hand'. The wetland office has since put the line on its map, and the crew gave the drone footage to the office for free, with no conditions at all.
source_title: 打字登山·自编新闻练习文 v1

textbook_series: 自编新闻练习材料（配合课堂打字训练，不绑定教材版本）
title: Twelve Lights on the Field
paragraphs: For four nights in October, a crew filmed a village football team in Qingyuan for a documentary. They set up twelve lights on stands six metres high, each run from a small generator, so the games could be filmed after dark. Nine families live within fifty metres of the field.

By the second night, the complaints had started. Light came through the curtains of a bedroom where a nurse slept before her shift. Another family said their chickens had stopped laying. One man stood at the fence and counted the lights out loud. Someone called the village office twice in one hour.

Ms Tan, who lives behind the goal, said, 'I do not hate the film. I work at night and I sleep in the day. Those lights turned my room into a classroom. I asked them to finish at ten, and they said the game was not over.'

The crew cut two lights and covered two more with black cloth. They finished at 10:40 instead of midnight, which cost them about forty minutes of play. The coach said the last part of the match was the best part, and now it was too dark. The village office asked both sides to write it down.

In the end, the film used mostly daylight training scenes and only three minutes of night play. The crew left the black cloth with the village office. A note on the box said the cloth fits lights of this size, and please use it next time.

textbook_series: 自编新闻练习材料（配合课堂打字训练，不绑定教材版本）
title: One Microphone in the Wet Market
paragraphs: A radio producer in Guangzhou spent eleven mornings in a wet market in Liwan. He recorded twenty-six hours of sound with one microphone and a cloth cover. He arrived at 5:50 each morning, before the fish stalls opened, and left at nine.

He did not ask people to speak. He asked them to work as usual. He stood three metres away and did not move for two hours. The microphone was between a chopping block and a drain, and it picked up knives, water, steel bowls, and a man calling prices in two languages at once.

The producer, Mr Ruan, said, 'The market has a rhythm. At six it is knives and water. At seven it is voices. At half past eight it is money and plastic bags. If you move the microphone one metre, you lose all of it.'

Two stallholders asked to be left out, and four hours of tape were erased. One asked for money. The market office wanted to read the script before the piece aired, and Mr Ruan said no, then agreed to play it to them instead. The money question was never settled, and the man still greets him coldly.

The finished piece is twenty-eight minutes long. The loudest sound in it is a metal bowl hit once, at 6:14, by accident. Three listeners wrote to the station. One said she had not been to that market in twenty years and knew exactly which stall it was. It was played twice, at noon and after midnight.
source_title: 打字登山·自编新闻练习文 v1

textbook_series: 自编新闻练习材料（配合课堂打字训练，不绑定教材版本）
title: The Word the Subtitles Got Wrong
paragraphs: A documentary about a village in eastern Guangdong had its first public showing in October. A language teacher in the audience stayed to the end and then wrote an email. The subtitles, she said, had translated the grandmother's word for cold as hungry.

The film team checked all fourteen minutes of subtitles again. They found nine more errors of the same kind. A word for a kind of basket had become a word for a boat. A joke about a neighbour had become an insult about his field. The team read each line aloud to a teacher from the village.

The director, Ms Shao, said, 'The grandmother was talking about the wind. She said the wind was cold enough to break a bowl. In the subtitles she was complaining about dinner. It was one small word, and it changed the whole scene.'

The film had already been sent to a festival in another city, and the deadline was in four days. Re-doing the subtitles cost 2,000 yuan. At first the director wanted to fix only the two worst lines. The editor said they should do all ten.

The new version came a day late and missed that festival. It was shown in the village hall in December, to ninety people. The grandmother's line about the wind is now the first sentence of the film, and she has heard it twice. The teacher who wrote the email came and sat in the front row.

textbook_series: 自编新闻练习材料（配合课堂打字训练，不绑定教材版本）
title: Filming From the Fourth Floor
paragraphs: On 16 September, a typhoon crossed the coast near Zhuhai with winds of about 140 kilometres an hour. A television crew of four had planned to report from the seawall. The station had booked the live slot a week earlier. Police closed the road at six in the morning, so that plan was gone.

The crew moved into a hotel and asked for a room on the sea side. The manager gave them a stairwell window on the fourth floor. It was safer but narrower. Two people could stand there, and the camera could not turn more than a little.

The reporter, Ms Kong, said, 'From the fourth floor the storm looked smaller. That was the problem. On the seawall you feel the wind push you. Up there you only see trees bend. I had to tell viewers that the camera was inside a building.'

Salt water got into the camera during a three-minute gap when the window was opened. Two lenses were ruined, and the repair cost about 6,000 yuan. The station also cut the live report from eight minutes to three because other crews had better pictures.

The three minutes that aired used eleven seconds of a tree bending almost to the ground. That shot came from the stairwell. The lenses were repaired in two weeks, and the crew now carries rain covers in every van, even in December. The station still uses that eleven seconds when it trains new reporters.
source_title: 打字登山·自编新闻练习文 v1
