textbook_series: 自编新闻练习材料（配合课堂打字训练，不绑定教材版本）
title: Four Hundred Bolts Before Breakfast
paragraphs: At 5:40 in the morning, Mr Gu stands on a bridge in Nansha with a hammer and a small mirror. He has 412 bolts to check on one section of steel. Below him, the water is forty-six metres down and the colour of wet concrete.

He works from a platform on two cables. The mirror lets him see the back of each bolt. He hits every bolt once and listens. A good bolt gives a clear note, and a loose one gives a dull sound, like a spoon on a box. The platform moves with the wind, and he works with it.

Mr Gu said, 'People think we look for cracks. Most days we listen. A crack you can see is already a big problem. A loose bolt tells you six months early, if you hit it in the right place and the wind is quiet enough. I have never found a crack that was safe to leave.'

One bolt near a joint above the third pier could not be reached without closing a lane. He asked for a closure in April and was refused twice, because the road carries ninety thousand cars a day. He waited three weeks for a forty-minute window, then brought a second lamp and a longer bar.

Three bolts were replaced, and one washer. His report runs to fourteen pages and includes sixty photographs. He walks about nine kilometres in a shift, most of it on steel. He is fifty-two and has done this work for nineteen years. The hammer was his father's.
source_title: 打字登山·自编新闻练习文 v1
license_or_permission: 本库自编，校内教学可自由使用

textbook_series: 自编新闻练习材料（配合课堂打字训练，不绑定教材版本）
title: Eight Samples a Shift
paragraphs: At six in the morning, Ms He takes the first water sample of her shift at a plant in Panyu. The plant sends about 240,000 tonnes of water to the city each day. She will take eight samples before six in the evening. The plant has not closed for a full day since 1998.

The water comes from a river two kilometres away. She tests for cloudiness, which should stay under 0.3. She checks the chlorine at 0.7 milligrams per litre, writes the number in a book, then on a screen, then says it aloud to a colleague. The samples go to a small lab next to the pump room.

Ms He said, 'The river tells you what kind of day it will be. After heavy rain it brings mud, and we add more. In winter it is clear and we add less. If you dose by the calendar instead of the river, you will be wrong in a week.'

In June a storm pushed the cloudiness to six times its normal level. She raised the dose twice and stayed by the valve. At two in the morning a pump stopped, and she and one colleague worked the valve by hand for two hours. The rain did not stop until four.

The finished water stayed inside its limits all night, and the tests are on file. She wrote three pages of notes before her shift ended. She has worked at the plant for eleven years, and her father worked there for twenty-six. Every page is signed by two people.
source_title: 打字登山·自编新闻练习文 v1
license_or_permission: 本库自编，校内教学可自由使用

textbook_series: 自编新闻练习材料（配合课堂打字训练，不绑定教材版本）
title: Four Hundred Loaves Before Six
paragraphs: Mr Pang turns on the first oven at 1:50 in the morning. By half past five, he and three bakers must finish 460 loaves for shops and one school. The bakery is on the ground floor of an old building, and the street is still dark. The shop opens at six sharp, and the first customers are waiting.

The dough was mixed at eight the night before and left to rise slowly. He weighs 26 kilograms of flour for the first batch, adds water at twelve degrees, and shapes each loaf by hand in about six seconds. The oven runs at 230 degrees.

Mr Pang said, 'The hard part is not the baking. It is the hour. At three in the morning your hands are slow and your head is empty. You must count the trays out loud, or you will put the same tray in twice. I have done it. You learn it in a month or you leave.'

At 3:10 the second oven lost heat. Thirty-four loaves came out flat and pale, and he threw them into a bin. The school had ordered 420 loaves and took 380. There was no time to bake more before the van left at 5:40. The bin was the only one that day, which he counted as luck.

The last tray came out at 5:26. He cleaned the bench, wrote the short order in a book, and went home at 6:10. He sleeps from seven until noon, then buys flour and checks the oven. His wife brings him tea at nine and says nothing about the hour.
source_title: 打字登山·自编新闻练习文 v1

textbook_series: 自编新闻练习材料（配合课堂打字训练，不绑定教材版本）
title: The Bus That Came Back at Ten
paragraphs: At ten at night, a bus rolls into a depot in Baiyun with a soft brake pedal. The mechanic, Mr Su, has thirty-two buses in the yard and one night to prepare them. The driver says the pedal went down too far at a crossing. The yard lights are the only thing moving at that hour.

He puts the bus over a pit and looks at the pads. The front left pad is down to two millimetres, and a rubber hose is wet near the joint. He writes 27 on a board, takes a lamp, and starts at the wheel. The pit is deep enough to stand in and warm from the engine.

Mr Su said, 'A soft pedal is a message. It can be air in the line, a bad hose, or a wheel that is not turning well. You cannot guess. You open it, you look, and you test it at walking speed before you touch the road. A good mechanic listens more than he looks.'

The new hose was not in the store, so he took one from bus 19, which was already finished. That bus then missed its 5:50 run, and the dispatcher argued with him for ten minutes. He said a good brake is worth more than a timetable.

He finished at 1:20 in the morning and wrote 118 checks on the sheet. He drove the bus twice around the yard at twenty kilometres an hour and stopped it four times. Then he signed the page and went to the next bus. The board with the number 27 comes off at the end of the shift.
source_title: 打字登山·自编新闻练习文 v1
license_or_permission: 本库自编，校内教学可自由使用

textbook_series: 自编新闻练习材料（配合课堂打字训练，不绑定教材版本）
title: The Corn Cob in the Dog
paragraphs: At 9:40 on a Monday, a vet in Tianhe opened a small dog on a steel table. The dog, a seven-year-old beagle, had eaten a corn cob two days before. It weighed twelve kilograms and had stopped drinking that morning. The clinic had already seen nineteen animals that day.

The X-ray at 8:15 showed a hard shape six centimetres long in the small intestine. The vet, Ms Xia, put in a tube for water and checked the heart twice. The tube went into a front leg, and the dog slept within a minute. The operation took forty minutes, and the piece came out in one move.

Ms Xia said, 'The cob does not break down. It goes through the stomach and stops where the tube is narrow. Every hour you wait, the wall gets thinner. By the time it breaks, the dog is in real danger and the work becomes much bigger.'

The owner first said no, because the operation cost 2,600 yuan. She wanted to wait until morning. Ms Xia said waiting was a risk and wrote the numbers on a card. Four hours later the dog was sick, and the owner called back and agreed. She said she had not slept the night before.

The dog went home two days later and ate rice on the third. The cob is in a glass jar on a shelf behind the desk, with the date on it. Ms Xia has eleven jars from this year, and six of them hold corn cobs. The owner sent a photo of the dog two weeks later.
source_title: 打字登山·自编新闻练习文 v1
license_or_permission: 本库自编，校内教学可自由使用

textbook_series: 自编新闻练习材料（配合课堂打字训练，不绑定教材版本）
title: Three Kilometres of White Line
paragraphs: At eleven at night, a crew of six closes one lane of a road in Zengcheng and begins to paint. The line will run 3.6 kilometres and be fifteen centimetres wide. Cars pass on the other side at sixty kilometres an hour, lit by orange lamps.

The paint is heated to about 190 degrees and comes out of a machine the men push at walking speed. Glass beads fall onto the wet line so it shines at night. The machine uses about twelve kilograms of paint for every hundred metres. A second man walks behind with a board and watches the line.

The crew leader, Mr Zeng, said, 'You cannot stop in the middle of a line. If you stop, the paint piles up and makes a bump. If you go too slow, the line is too thick and peels in a month. Your feet must keep the same speed for an hour.'

Rain began at one in the morning. Eight hundred metres of fresh line had to be covered with cloth, and the crew sat in the van for two hours. The road had to reopen at 5:30, so they finished 1.1 kilometres short and drove back with half a load of paint.

They returned the next night and the night after that. The whole job took four nights. A taxi driver stopped at the end and said the new line was brighter than the old one in the rain. Mr Zeng wrote that in his book. The old line is still under the new one, and nobody will see it.
source_title: 打字登山·自编新闻练习文 v1
license_or_permission: 本库自编，校内教学可自由使用

textbook_series: 自编新闻练习材料（配合课堂打字训练，不绑定教材版本）
title: Forty-Two Thousand Letters
paragraphs: At eight in the evening, Ms Xia starts her shift at a sorting centre in Huadu. Until four in the morning, fourteen people move 42,000 letters and 9,000 small parcels. The hall is the size of two basketball courts and smells of paper and tape.

A machine reads the postcodes and sends each letter down one of thirty-six boxes. It handles about 8,000 letters an hour. Anything it cannot read falls into a bin, and a person reads the address and writes the code by hand. Most of the letters come from offices, and a few are hand-written.

Ms Xia said, 'A machine is fast but it is not careful. It reads a six as an eight and sends a letter to the other side of the city. We catch most of them. The ones we miss come back in a week, and someone has waited for nothing. The machine does not know the difference.'

At eleven the label printer failed. Two thousand three hundred letters waited in a bin. The supervisor wanted to call in two more workers, and the manager said the cost was too high for one night. They wrote codes by hand for ninety minutes.

The last bag was tied at 3:50. Ms Xia walks about eleven kilometres inside the hall each night, and her shoes last four months. She keeps one letter with no address in her bag. It has been there since March, and she still reads it. She has read it twice, but there is no name inside.
source_title: 打字登山·自编新闻练习文 v1
license_or_permission: 本库自编，校内教学可自由使用

textbook_series: 自编新闻练习材料（配合课堂打字训练，不绑定教材版本）
title: Two and a Half Tonnes of Sheets
paragraphs: At seven in the morning, Mr Lou opens the door of a hospital laundry and counts the bags. Today there are 2.6 tonnes of sheets, towels and gowns, and eight machines to wash them. The first truck from the wards arrives at 7:20. The laundry is in the basement, and the air is warm and wet.

Every sheet is washed at 70 degrees for twelve minutes, then pressed between rollers at 160 degrees. A hole the size of a coin sends a sheet to a pile that will be cut into cloths. About forty sheets a day end up in that pile. The pile goes to the cleaning team on the second floor.

Mr Lou said, 'People think we wash cloth. We wash time. A ward cannot wait, and a sheet with a stain is not clean even if it is warm. If we are two hours late, someone upstairs is making a bed with nothing in their hands.'

At ten, the second machine stopped with 600 kilograms still inside. The hospital said it could not take fewer sheets that day. The team ran two extra hours, and one worker burned his hand on a pipe. He kept working with a bandage. Mr Lou moved people to the third machine and worked the door himself.

The last bag went out at 6:40 in the evening. Seventeen sheets were thrown away, and the number on his list matched the number in the truck. Mr Lou has worked here for sixteen years and still checks the number twice.
source_title: 打字登山·自编新闻练习文 v1
license_or_permission: 本库自编，校内教学可自由使用

textbook_series: 自编新闻练习材料（配合课堂打字训练，不绑定教材版本）
title: The Nest in the Ninth Tree
paragraphs: At 7:30 in the morning, a crew of four stops a truck under a power line in Conghua. The line carries 11,000 volts. Their job is to cut back the branches of forty-two trees before dark, so that wind and rain cannot push a branch onto the wire.

Mr Ku goes up in a bucket that lifts him eight metres. He wears gloves that are tested every six months and uses a saw with a long handle. He cuts in small pieces, and a second man on the ground pulls each piece away with a rope. The bucket has a control stick and moves slowly.

Mr Ku said, 'You do not cut the big branch first. You cut the small ones, and you watch which way the weight is leaning. A branch that falls the wrong way can take the wire with it. It can also hit the man below. I have seen a branch fall on a parked car.'

At the ninth tree, a nest with three eggs sat on a branch that had to go. Work stopped for an hour while a colleague called a wildlife office. The office said to leave that branch until the eggs were gone, so the crew left it for later.

They finished thirty-eight trees and left four for the next week. The power stayed on all day, which is the point of the job and also the reason nobody notices it. Mr Ku has done this for fourteen years and has never been badly hurt. The four trees were done the following Tuesday, and the nest was empty.
source_title: 打字登山·自编新闻练习文 v1
license_or_permission: 本库自编，校内教学可自由使用

textbook_series: 自编新闻练习材料（配合课堂打字训练，不绑定教材版本）
title: One Hundred and Seventy-Six Meters
paragraphs: At ten past eight, Ms Yan reads meters in an old district of Liwan. Her list has 176 addresses, six buildings without lifts, and eleven kilometres of walking. She carries a hand-held device and paper notices. Her round starts near the river and ends at the main road. She has done this round for nine years.

Most meters take three minutes: open the box, read five numbers, photograph the dial, and press the button. The old buildings take longer. On the ninth floor of one block, the meter is behind a bicycle and a bag of rice, and the light has failed.

Ms Yan said, 'I know this district by its doors. Number 12 has a dog that is loud but friendly. Number 30 has a gate that sticks in the rain. The numbers do not open the doors, so I have to remember the doors as well. It saves time.'

At 4:30 she had fourteen meters left and two locked gates. One resident said his bill was too high and would not let her in. She showed him the reading from last month, and he closed the door. She read the other twelve and came back at six.

She sent 162 readings and estimated 14. The estimates are marked in the system with a small letter, and the next reading will correct them. She walked about twelve kilometres. Her shoes are replaced every five months, and most of the old ones are still good for the garden.
source_title: 打字登山·自编新闻练习文 v1
license_or_permission: 本库自编，校内教学可自由使用

textbook_series: 自编新闻练习材料（配合课堂打字训练，不绑定教材版本）
title: The Machine That Marked Two Hundred Essays
paragraphs: In October, a middle school in Zengcheng let a marking system grade two hundred essays from three grade 8 classes. The system was on trial for one term and cost 10,000 yuan. It read each essay in about four seconds and gave a score out of twenty.

The teachers read the same papers first and wrote their own marks in pencil. When the two sets were compared, the system agreed with the teachers on 122 of the 200 essays. On the other 78, the gap was often three points or more, and on six papers it was eight points.

Two results worried the teachers most. A paper of forty words with one long quotation scored 17, while a careful essay about a grandmother's shop scored 8 because most of its sentences were short. Ms Tan said, "It counts long words, not thinking. My quietest student wrote the best page of the term."

The school asked for a refund for the second half of the term and got 5,000 yuan back. The company said the system learned from corrections and would improve. The head of the English department said the school could not wait for it to learn on students, and the trial was cut short.

Since November the system has checked spelling and punctuation only, and a teacher marks the writing. It also prints a list of every sentence longer than thirty words. Ms Tan says the list is useful, because it shows her what to teach next. "The machine is good at counting," she said. "I am paid to read."
source_title: 打字登山·自编新闻练习文 v1
license_or_permission: 本库自编，校内教学可自由使用

textbook_series: 自编新闻练习材料（配合课堂打字训练，不绑定教材版本）
title: The Camera That Counted Too Many People
paragraphs: On a wet Friday in September, a camera at the north gate of a night market in Panyu counted 8,400 visitors between six and nine in the evening. The market manager, Mr Guo, knew the number was wrong before he finished his tea. His own staff had counted about 5,100.

The camera was installed in July to help plan the market's night bus. It stands 2.8 metres above the gate and counts heads that cross a white line on the pavement. On dry evenings its numbers matched the gate staff within five percent, and the market began to trust it.

Rain changed the picture. Umbrellas looked like heads, and the wet pavement reflected them, so the camera counted many people twice. "We sent fourteen extra staff and a second bus to a market that did not need them," Mr Guo said. "The bus left half empty at ten."

The mistake cost 3,000 yuan in wages and bus fees. Two stallholders also complained, because the extra barriers blocked the way to their tables for two hours. The camera company sent a technician, who tested the gate on three dry nights and found nothing wrong with it.

In October the camera was raised to 3.5 metres, and a line was painted one metre before the gate so that people walk through it one by one. On the next wet Friday it counted 5,380 against a gate count of 5,050. Mr Guo still puts two students with clickers at the gate when it rains.
source_title: 打字登山·自编新闻练习文 v1
license_or_permission: 本库自编，校内教学可自由使用

textbook_series: 自编新闻练习材料（配合课堂打字训练，不绑定教材版本）
title: The Voice Box in the Lift Lobby
paragraphs: In July, a housing estate in Liwan put a small voice box in the lift lobby of its oldest block. Sixty-two residents there are over seventy. The box was meant to let them call a family member, ask for the doctor, or report a broken light without finding a phone number first.

The estate paid 18,000 yuan for twelve boxes, one for each block, and six weeks of testing. In the first six weeks, residents used the box 1,140 times. About 340 of those attempts failed, mostly because the box did not understand the local dialect spoken by the oldest residents.

Ms He, who is seventy-eight and has lived in the block for forty years, tried to report a broken lift light four times. The box heard "light" and offered to turn on her kitchen light. On the fifth try she walked to the office instead. "I said the words I say to my neighbour," she said.

The estate could not add the dialect quickly. The company wanted 9,000 yuan more and eight weeks, and the committee argued about the price for two meetings. In the end, a younger neighbour recorded 260 common phrases in the local dialect, and the company loaded them without charge.

The failure rate fell to about nine percent. The estate also added a button that calls the office directly, and that button is now used more than the voice commands. Ms He uses the button. She says the box is better than nothing, but she still calls her son, because he answers in one sentence.

title: The Bin That Sent Batteries to the Wrong Side
paragraphs: For three weeks in May, a sorting machine stood beside the bins of a housing estate in Tianhe. It has one arm, one camera and six openings: paper, plastic, metal, glass, kitchen waste and other waste. The estate hoped it would cut the time staff spent sorting bags by hand.

The machine sorted about 2,600 items during the trial. It was right on 2,290 of them, about 88 percent, which the company called a good result, but the 310 wrong items included things that were a danger to the staff who emptied the bins.

Its worst mistake was batteries. Forty-three small batteries went into the kitchen waste opening, because their round shape and grey colour looked like bottle caps. The arm pressed them with the rest of the waste, and two of them broke open. A worker smelled smoke and emptied the bag onto the pavement.

The company's technician, Mr Xia, said the camera had never been taught to look for batteries. "We trained it on bottles, paper and tins," he said. "We never gave it a picture of a battery, so it put them where the shape fit. That is what it was asked to do."

The trial ended with a new rule. Batteries now go into a red box by the office door, and a person stands beside the machine for two hours each morning. With the person there, accuracy rose to 96 percent. Without one, it fell back to 88. The estate kept the machine for the morning shift only.

title: A Translator at the Clinic Window
paragraphs: In April, a clinic in Haizhu tested a hand-held translator at its front window for three weeks. The clinic serves about four hundred patients a day, and its two nurses often need help with patients who speak only Cantonese or English. The device was rented for 6,000 yuan.

The translator was used in 240 conversations. It handled directions well: which floor, which room, how long the wait. It did less well with numbers. In nineteen conversations the nurses found an error, and three of those errors were about medicine, which the clinic reported the same week.

The worst case involved a visitor from another province who needed a cream for a skin rash. The nurse said "use it twice a day", and the device said "use it twelve times a day" in Cantonese. The nurse heard the number, stopped, and wrote the instruction on a card instead.

Nurse Liang said the device was useful for the queue and the waiting room, but not for anything a patient would take home. "A wrong floor costs a walk upstairs," she said. "A wrong number on a cream costs a week of skin." The clinic argued with the supplier about who should pay for the errors.

The clinic kept the translator for directions only. All medicine instructions are now written on a printed card in four languages, and a nurse reads the card aloud before the patient leaves. In May the clinic used the device 190 times and recorded no medicine errors. Each card costs about two yuan.

title: The Robot That Could Not Climb Three Steps
paragraphs: In March, a housing estate in Baiyun rented a delivery robot for 2,000 yuan a month. The robot carried parcels from the gate to the buildings, a walk of about six hundred metres, and was supposed to save the two gate guards forty trips a day. It arrived with a small flag on its back.

The first route took twenty-two minutes, not six. Three steps at the entrance to the oldest building stopped the robot completely. It stood still, rang a bell, and waited for someone to lift it. On the first day the guards lifted it eleven times and stopped answering the bell after lunch.

On the fourth day the robot blocked the door of building six for forty minutes while a resident tried to carry a bed frame outside. The resident, Mr Feng, said, "I asked it to move and it said please wait. I waited, and then I carried the bed around it. It is polite and it is useless."

The estate asked for a ramp, but the steps belong to the building, and the residents of the ground floor did not want a metal slope outside their windows. The argument lasted three weeks and two meetings. A ramp was finally built from a wooden board, which cost 700 yuan.

The robot now runs only on the flat path between the gate and buildings one to five, a route of three hundred metres. It makes about fifty trips a day and still needs a person at the gate to load it. The guards say it saves them an hour. They also say they could walk that hour faster.

title: The Hotline That Invented an Opening Time
paragraphs: A library in Yuexiu added a chat hotline in February. Readers could type a question on the library's page and get an answer in seconds. In five weeks the hotline received 3,900 questions, about a hundred a day, and answered 82 percent of them without a person.

Most questions were simple: whether a book was on the shelf, when the children's room closed, and whether a book could be returned at another branch. The hotline did well on these, but then it began to fill gaps in its own answers, which the librarian, Ms Qiu, had not expected from a machine.

On a Sunday it told eleven readers that the library opened at eight on Monday. The library opens at nine, and the Monday morning is used for cleaning. About sixty people came before nine and stood outside in the rain. A reader showed the guard her phone, and the guard did not know what to say.

Ms Qiu read the hotline's answers for a week and found nine wrong opening times. "It was not lying on purpose," she said. "It had read a notice about our summer hours and mixed the two. Nobody had told it that summer ended." The library wrote new rules for the hotline in three days.

Since April the hotline answers only shelf questions and passes everything else to a person, who replies after nine. The waiting time is longer, about four hours on a busy day. Complaints fell from forty a week to six. Ms Qiu says she would rather be slow and right.

title: The Orchard That Was Watered Three Times
paragraphs: In June, a lychee orchard in Conghua buried forty soil sensors under twelve mu of trees. The sensors were connected to a pump and a small box that watered the trees when the soil became dry. The farmer, Mr Luo, paid 9,800 yuan for the system and a year of service.

For two weeks it worked well. The box watered at night, when less water is lost to the sun, and Mr Luo slept through the watering for the first time in years. Then a heavy storm washed mud over one sensor on the eastern slope, and the mud dried into a hard cap.

The buried sensor read dry soil and asked for water. The other sensors read wet soil and asked for none. The box followed the driest one, which is a sensible rule on a normal day. It watered the whole eastern slope three times between midnight and four in the morning.

About 8,000 litres ran onto the slope, and the pump pulled air for forty minutes before Mr Luo woke and switched it off. The repair cost 3,400 yuan for a new pump. "The box did what I told it," Mr Luo said. "The problem is that I told it to trust one voice."

He changed the setting so that two sensors must agree before the pump starts. He also dug a small drain and put a cover over each sensor. In July the system watered nine times and the pump did not fail. Mr Luo still walks the eastern slope after every storm, with a spade over his shoulder.

title: The Gate That Did Not Know the Twins
paragraphs: A swimming pool in Huangpu replaced its paper cards with a face-scan gate in May. The pool has 1,240 members, and the gate was meant to let them in without stopping at the desk. The pool paid 40,000 yuan for two gates and a year of service.

The gate worked for most adults and failed for about seven people a day. Wet hair, fogged glasses and children who looked up at the camera all caused a red light. On busy evenings the queue reached the car park, and the desk opened a side door to let people through without scanning.

The strangest case was a pair of twins, aged ten, who swim on Tuesdays. The gate learned one face and let both boys in on the same name for three weeks. Their mother noticed when the pool's entry record showed her son had swum nine times in a month.

The pool manager, Ms Wen, said the gate was not wrong often, but it was wrong in ways that members remembered. "A card can be lost and replaced in a minute," she said. "A face is not a card. When the gate says no, the person feels that the pool does not know them."

Since July members have used a card and a face together. If the two do not match, the gate stays shut and the desk presses a button after checking the card. Entry takes about four seconds longer per person. The pool says complaints have almost stopped, and the twins now have separate cards.

title: The Voice That Read the Morning News
paragraphs: In September, a middle school in Huadu replaced its student announcer with a synthetic voice for the morning notices. The voice read the timetable, the weather, and the names of students who had lost things. It cost 3,000 yuan a year and it never arrived late.

The first week went well. The voice read the lunch menu and the bus times clearly, and the office no longer needed a student to miss ten minutes of class. Then it began to meet names it did not know. In three weeks it mispronounced fourteen students and two teachers.

One name came out as a different word with a rude meaning, and the corridor laughed for a week. The student, a grade 7 boy, asked the office to stop reading his name. The office agreed, and from then on the voice read only the class and the lost item, never the person.

The music teacher, Mr Shen, argued that the voice should be dropped. The head of the office argued that it saved a student ten minutes a day and cost less than a microphone. They compromised: the voice reads the timetable and the weather, and a student reads everything with a name in it.

The student announcer came back in November, four mornings a week. The voice still reads the Friday notices, when the list is long and nobody wants to miss class. A grade 8 girl who reads on Mondays practises on Sunday night. "The voice is faster," she said, "but it cannot say sorry when it reads a name wrong."

title: The Trail That Stopped Seven Hundred Metres Short
paragraphs: On the first of May, a new walking trail opened in Conghua. It runs 6.4 kilometres from a village road to a small waterfall, and it took eleven months to build. The district expected about three hundred walkers on a normal weekend, and printed that number in its notice.

By the end of May, the trail had received 4,900 visitors, and the car park at the village held only forty cars. On the third weekend, cars stood along the road for two kilometres. A villager opened her yard for parking and charged ten yuan, and by June four more yards were doing the same.

Then the rain came. A storm on 12 June brought down a tree and about thirty cubic metres of soil across the last section. The final seven hundred metres, which includes two wooden bridges and the best view of the waterfall, were closed. The rest of the trail stayed open.

Repair was slower than the build, because the soil above the path was still moving and the engineers would not send workers under it. They waited nineteen days for a dry week, then built a stone wall four metres high. The wall cost 260,000 yuan, more than the two wooden bridges had cost together.

The trail reopened on 20 August with a new rule: no entry after three in the afternoon, and a limit of two hundred people a day. The village now has a small booth and two counters. "We wanted visitors," said Mr Deng, who farms beside the trail. "We did not want the hill to come down on them."

title: Nine Minutes Off the Ferry
paragraphs: On 1 July, a passenger ferry between an island in Nansha and the mainland began using a new pier. The crossing fell from twenty-two minutes to thirteen. The pier and the dredging cost 8.6 million yuan and took two years, mostly because the river mouth is shallow and the work could only be done at high tide.

The ferry carries about nine hundred people a day and runs fourteen times in each direction. Before the new pier, the boat had to wait for the tide twice a day, and the last crossing sometimes left forty minutes late. Islanders who work on the mainland missed the first bus and the first meeting of the morning.

The shorter route has a cost. The boat now passes closer to a fishing ground, and the wash from its engine reaches the mud where clams are farmed. Mr He, who has farmed clams there for twenty-two years, said the young clams were being pushed out of the mud and into deeper water.

The ferry company measured the wash and agreed to slow down over a stretch of four hundred metres. The slow section adds ninety seconds to the trip. "Nine minutes is nine minutes," Mr He said. "I am not asking for the old pier. I am asking for a boat that goes slower near my mud."

The company also paid 30,000 yuan for new ropes and posts around the clam beds. The ferry has run on the new timetable for four months, and late crossings have fallen from eleven a week to one. Mr He says the clams are better, but he will not know for certain until next summer.

title: The Tunnel That Met Fifteen Metres Off Line
paragraphs: A road tunnel through a hill in Zengcheng was dug from both ends at the same time. The tunnel is 2.1 kilometres long, and the plan was for the two teams to meet in the middle in March. Each team dug about three metres a day, working in three shifts around the clock.

They met on 18 March, but not in the right place. The two headings missed each other by fifteen metres, and one was almost a metre higher than the other. The mistake was found when a surveyor checked the line from above the hill, using a receiver on a long pole.

The cause was a survey stone that had moved. A stone marker on the hill had been knocked about forty centimetres by a machine in the first month, and every measurement after that carried the error. Nobody had checked the stone again, because it was set in concrete and looked permanent.

Joining the two headings took eleven more days. Workers dug a small side passage by hand, then widened it with a machine. The extra work cost about 400,000 yuan. The project manager, Mr Tan, said, "We trusted one stone for five months. The stone was wrong on the first day."

The tunnel opened in June, three months late. Before the tunnel, the road over the hill took twenty-five minutes in good weather and closed in fog. The new road takes four minutes. Drivers use it every day, and most of them have no idea that the two halves were once almost a metre apart.

title: The Hill That Was Forty Metres Wrong
paragraphs: For two years, a walking map of a hill in Conghua put the summit forty metres west of where it is. The map was printed on a board at the car park and copied by three walking apps. About six thousand people climb the hill each year, and many of them start in the late afternoon.

The error was small on paper and large on the ground. The false summit is a flat rock above a steep drop, and walkers who followed the map at dusk often found themselves on the wrong side of the ridge. In eighteen months, rescue teams were called out twelve times to bring people down.

Last October, a surveyor, Ms Lin, walked the ridge with a hand-held receiver for two days. She took readings at nine points and found that the highest point was forty metres east and three metres higher. She also found that the board had copied a map drawn in 1998, before the path was moved.

The district replaced the board in January, at a cost of 4,200 yuan, and wrote to the three app makers. Two changed their maps within a month. The third said the change was in a queue and took five months. In that time, two more walkers were led to the wrong rock after dark.

The new board has a large arrow and the words "summit, forty metres east". It also has a small note explaining that the old map was wrong. Ms Lin says she would like every map to carry the date it was surveyed. "A map is not a picture," she said. "It is a promise about where things are."

title: The Viewpoint That Closed After Six Hundred Visitors
paragraphs: A viewpoint on a hill in Panyu closed on 1 August after four months of heavy use. The platform is twelve metres long and was built for about eighty people at a time. On weekends in July, volunteers counted more than six hundred visitors in a single day, most of them between four and seven in the evening.

The damage was mostly to the ground around the platform. Visitors had walked around the fence to reach a rock for photographs, and the grass on the slope had gone. After a storm in July, a strip of soil about thirty metres long slid down the hill and stopped at a path below.

The district closed the platform and the path below it. A sign said the hill would reopen when the slope was safe. Local walkers were angry, because the viewpoint was the only place on the hill with a clear view of the river and no trees in the way. Two of them wrote to the district office.

An engineer, Mr Xia, said the slope could be fixed with a stone wall and a new path, but the work would take four months and cost 700,000 yuan. "The rock was never the problem," he said. "The problem was six hundred people standing on a slope built for eighty."

The viewpoint reopened in December with a wooden walkway 300 metres long and a fence that cannot be climbed without a ladder. Numbers are limited to 150 people at a time, and two volunteers count at the entrance. On the first weekend, 140 people came. The walk is longer and the view is the same.

title: The Bridge That Goes Under at High Tide
paragraphs: A low stone bridge crosses a river mouth on an island in Nansha. Twice a day the tide covers it, sometimes by half a metre. For years, people crossed when they could and waited when they could not, and nobody wrote down the times. Visitors often arrived at the wrong hour and sat in their cars.

In April, the village put a board at each end of the bridge with the tide times for the month. The times came from a gauge installed under the bridge, which records the water level every ten minutes. The board is changed on the first day of each month by a retired teacher, Mr Liang.

The first board was wrong by about twenty minutes, because the gauge sat at the wrong height above the water. An old fisherman noticed, because he had crossed that bridge for fifty years and knew the tide by the weeds on the third stone. "I know the tide by the weeds," he told Mr Liang.

The gauge was fixed in May, and the board now gives a safe window rather than a single time. On most days the bridge is dry for about nine hours, in two periods. Mr Liang writes the windows in large numbers and adds one line: do not cross when the water is above the second stone.

The board has changed how people use the bridge. The school bus now crosses at ten past seven, when the water is low, instead of at eight. Fishermen say fewer cars are stranded. In June, two visitors ignored the board and waited on the bridge for an hour with their shopping. Mr Liang wrote that down too.

title: The Shelter That Faced the Wrong Way
paragraphs: A new bus shelter on a road in Huadu opened in March and faced the hillside. The glass back of the shelter, which was meant to block the wind, stood between the waiting passengers and the road. To see a bus coming, people had to stand outside in the rain or step into the road.

The shelter cost 46,000 yuan and replaced an old one with a metal roof and no walls. The workers built it according to a drawing that showed the road on the other side. The road had been moved eight metres east in 2019, when a new lane was added, and the drawing had never been changed.

About two hundred people use the stop each morning, including students from a nearby school. For four months they waited on the pavement in the sun and the rain, and some stood in the road to see the bus. A resident, Ms Zou, collected 340 signatures asking for the shelter to be turned around.

The transport office first said the shelter was correct and the drawing was the problem, which did not help anyone. Then it said turning the shelter would cost 9,000 yuan and might break the glass. In July it agreed to pay, after a bus driver reported that passengers were stepping into the road.

The shelter was turned in one day in August. The glass now faces the hill, and the open side faces the road. The old holes in the pavement were filled with concrete, which left four grey patches. "The patches are ugly and the waiting is better," Ms He said. The driver can see the queue now.

title: Eleven Hundred Steps Through the Tea Fields
paragraphs: In the tea hills above a village in Conghua, a path of 1,100 stone steps now runs from the village square to a spring. Before this year, the path was mud, and after rain it was a stream. The steps were cut and laid by a team of nine workers in seven months.

Each step is about 1.2 metres wide and 15 centimetres high, which is low enough for an old person to climb without stopping. The stone came from a quarry nine kilometres away, and the trucks could not reach the top of the hill, so the last 400 metres were carried up by hand.

The village paid 380,000 yuan, most of it from a fund for village roads. Some tea farmers objected, because the path crosses two rows of their bushes. The village moved the path twelve metres west, which added sixty steps. "We were told on the day the stones arrived," said Mr Pan, who owns one of the rows.

The spring at the top now has a stone basin and a sign that says the water is not for drinking without boiling. In the first three months, about 1,800 people walked the path, including 300 who came on a single Saturday in October. The village shop sold 400 bottles of water that month.

The steps have made one thing harder. The old mud path was soft, and pickers carried baskets down without looking. Stone is hard on the knees. Ms Luo, sixty-four, who picks tea on the hill, uses the steps going up and the old path going down. "The stone is quicker," she said, "and my knees liked the mud."

title: The Ferry That Used the Wrong Tide Table
paragraphs: For two years, a small ferry to an island in Nansha used the tide table of a port thirty kilometres away. The tables are not the same: the tide at the island comes about forty minutes later. The ferry's first crossing left at seven, and on some days the water in the channel was too low.

The boat drew 1.4 metres of water, and the channel at the island pier was dredged to 1.8 metres. When the ferry left on the wrong tide, it touched the bottom. Between 2024 and this spring, the boat ran aground nine times, twice with passengers aboard who had to be taken off by a small boat.

Nobody connected the groundings to the table, because the boat usually got through. A new captain, Mr Wu, began to write down the time, the water level and the number of passengers on every crossing. After forty crossings he saw that the groundings came in groups of two or three days.

He compared his notes with the tide table and found the forty-minute gap. The ferry company checked with the harbour office, which confirmed that the island's tide is later. "The table was not wrong," Mr Wu said. "It was right for a place that was not here."

Since May the ferry has used a tide gauge at the island pier, read by the ticket seller each morning. The first crossing now leaves at 7:40 when the tide is low, and the timetable has two versions, one for spring tides and one for neap tides. There have been no groundings in five months.

title: The Road on the Map That Is a Rice Field
paragraphs: For about a year, a mapping app sent drivers down a farm track in Zengcheng that ends in a rice field. The track is 1.6 kilometres long, wide enough for one car, and has no place to turn. The app showed it as a road connecting two villages, and gave it a name.

The track was built in 2018 for a small truck that carried fertiliser. It was never a public road, and the two villages are connected by a road three kilometres longer. Drivers who followed the app found the field, stopped, and had to reverse the whole way in the dark.

The village head, Mr Deng, counted forty cars in one month last summer. Some drivers damaged the edge of the field, and one car slid into the mud after rain and had to be pulled out by a tractor for 300 yuan. The village put a wooden sign at the entrance, but the app still sent people.

In October a student from the village, who was learning to make maps, reported the track to the app. She sent four photos, the position of the sign, and a note saying the track is not open to cars. The app changed the map in eleven days. "It was easy," she said. "Nobody had told them."

The village has painted "farm track, no cars" on a board two metres wide. The app shows the track as a footpath, which it is for most of the year. Mr Deng says about five cars still come each month, usually at night, and the tractor driver now charges 400 yuan.

title: Nine Hundred Metres of Drain Behind the Market
paragraphs: On the first Saturday in March, forty volunteers began clearing a drain behind a wet market in Haizhu. The drain runs 900 metres to a river channel and was last opened eleven years ago. After heavy rain it backed up and pushed dirty water into six vegetable stalls at the front.

Most of the work was done by hand with spades and buckets, because the lane is too narrow for a machine. The team lifted 2.3 tonnes of black mud and 140 kilograms of plastic bags and broken bowls. Two men spent three hours inside the pipe, with bicycle lamps tied to their heads.

The worst place was halfway along, where a tree root had grown through two concrete rings and held a mattress. Behind the root the team pulled out a bicycle wheel and eleven bags of wet leaves. Mr Pan, who has sold fish here since 1998, said the smell used to keep customers away.

The district gave 12,000 yuan for tools and a pump, but the money arrived in May, two months after the work began. Until then the volunteers used an old pump borrowed from a building site two streets away. A shop owner complained about mud on the road, so the team washed the lane every evening.

By June, after a storm, water ran through the drain in forty minutes instead of six hours. The market paid 3,400 yuan for a metal grill with three-centimetre gaps at the entrance. The committee now checks the drain twice a year, in March and in September, whether it looks blocked or not.

title: The Factory That Washed Bottles With Rain
paragraphs: A drinks factory in Panyu cut its water use by 38 percent last year, after it began washing bottles with rain. The factory fills about 900,000 bottles a day and used 1,850 tonnes of water a month. By March it was using 1,150 tonnes a month, and the bill fell with it.

The idea came from an engineer, Ms Su, who noticed that the last rinse was almost clean. The factory now collects rain from 2,000 square metres of roof into four steel tanks. That water does the first wash, and the last rinse is pumped back to the start of the next load.

The system cost 260,000 yuan and took five months to fit, mostly at night so the lines kept running. Its first week went badly, because one tank still held soap from the wash before it. Twelve thousand bottles came out with a faint smell, and a customer in Dongguan sent the order back.

The factory lost 40,000 yuan on that order, and the owner nearly stopped the whole project. Ms Su argued for one more month, and the team added a second filter and a rinse before each fill. "We were cleaning the water and forgetting the box that it sat in," Ms Su said.

Since June the factory has saved about 700 tonnes a month, and the system should pay for itself in four years. In the dry season it still buys treated water from a drinks factory next door. Ms Su wants a second roof tank, but the roof is already full of pipes.

title: A Staircase for Fish at the Old Weir
paragraphs: In April, workers finished a fish ladder beside an old weir on a river in Conghua. The weir is 3.2 metres high, and it has held the river back since 1971. Fish that once swam upstream to lay eggs had not been seen above it for thirty years.

The ladder is a concrete channel 26 metres long, divided into 22 small pools with quiet water. Each pool is 12 centimetres higher than the one before, so a fish can rest between jumps. The whole thing cost 480,000 yuan and took seven months, most of it in the dry season.

The first design did not work, and the reason was the speed of the water. Water rushed down the channel too fast, and a camera at the top recorded only eleven fish in three weeks. The engineers slowed the flow and added stones to make quiet corners behind each step.

Mr Luo, who has fished this river since 1994, said he was not surprised by the slow start. "The fish are small, and a young carp cannot swim through water that runs like a tap," he said. The second design cut the speed by half, and it cost 60,000 yuan more than the first.

By June the camera counted 380 fish in one night, mostly carp and one kind of small silver fish. Nobody has yet seen the eels that the older villagers still remember from their own childhood. The district now checks the ladder twice a month and clears leaves from the pools.

title: The Week the Water Tasted of Pipes
paragraphs: For eleven days in May, taps in part of Baiyun gave water that smelled and tasted of new pipes. The plant that serves the area had just replaced its filters, and it restarted them two months early. About 90,000 people live on that supply, and most of them noticed the change at once.

The plant spent 3.2 million yuan on filters made of a black material that must be washed for six weeks. The plant washed them for only two weeks, because the old filters were already failing. On the first morning the water came out grey, then cleared, but the taste stayed.

The hotline took 240 calls in three days, and most of them came in the first morning. Most callers said the water smelled of a swimming pool, and a few said it made tea taste strange. Tests showed nothing harmful, and the plant said so in a notice on the second day.

Not everyone believed the notice, and the shops near the gate were the first to act. One shop sold 400 large bottles in a day, and a school sent a driver out for ice. Ms Feng, who lives on the fourth floor, boiled water for her son but still gave him bottled water for a week.

The plant now flushes new filters for the full six weeks and sends a text message before any change. Twelve residents taste the water every Friday morning, and each writes down what they notice. The taste was normal again by 21 May, and the plant has kept the tasting group since then.

title: Two Thousand Bottles on a River Beach
paragraphs: On 12 April, 260 volunteers spent three hours cleaning a beach on an island in Nansha, where the river meets the sea. They filled 780 bags and weighed them at the car park: 2,140 kilograms in total, of which 1,330 were plastic bottles.

The beach is 1.6 kilometres long and faces the shipping channel, so rubbish arrives with every high tide. The team worked in four lines, from the water to the grass, and left a marker every hundred metres. No truck could reach the sand, so every bag was carried 900 metres by hand.

About 40 percent of the bottles were less than a year old, judged by the dates printed on the labels. The oldest was a soy sauce bottle from 2009, and it was still whole after fifteen years. A student who kept the count said the dates made the rubbish feel less like weather and more like people.

The clean-up cost 9,000 yuan, mostly for gloves, bags and the hire of a truck. Two volunteers were cut by glass and had to stop, and the tide came in at half past eleven. The far end of the beach was still full, so the team left the last 300 metres for another day.

A second clean-up in May covered that 300 metres and collected 410 kilograms, about a fifth of the first total. The organiser, Ms Kuang, said the smaller number did not mean the beach was getting cleaner. "It means the river is still bringing it in, and we are cleaning a beach, not a tap," she said.

title: The Leak Under the Running Track
paragraphs: In February, a science group at a middle school in Yuexiu found a broken water pipe under the running track. The group had read the school's water meter every night at ten for a month. On nineteen of the thirty nights, the meter moved while every tap in the school was closed.

The numbers were small at first: about 0.4 cubic metres an hour, or six tonnes a night. The group checked the toilets, the kitchen and the garden taps, and found nothing wrong. Then a student noticed that the ground beside the long jump pit was soft even in dry weather.

The school did not believe the finding at once, and asked for a second look. A worker dug beside the wrong pipe and spent 2,000 yuan and a day on a drain that was working well. The second dig, four metres along the track, found a joint that had cracked and was losing water into the soil.

The repair cost 8,000 yuan and closed the track for four days, which meant two classes of PE moved into the hall. The group's teacher, Ms Yan, said the school asked why nobody had noticed it before. "The water went under the ground, so nobody had to step in it," she said.

The leak was losing about 2,200 tonnes a year, close to what the school uses in a month. The June bill was 1,900 yuan lower than the bill for the same month a year before. The group still reads the meter on the first Monday of each month and writes the number on a board.

title: The Pond That Turned Green in June
paragraphs: In June, fish began to die in a village pond near Huadu, and nobody knew why. The pond is about 1,400 square metres and sits between three vegetable plots and a row of houses. Within a week the water had turned the colour of green paint, and the smell reached the bus stop.

The village tested the water and found very little oxygen in it, even near the surface. Three small farms had been washing fertiliser bags at the edge, and a pipe from two houses carried soapy water in. Mud at the bottom had stored years of this, and the hot weather released it.

The clean-up cost 380,000 yuan, paid in part by the village and in part by the district. Workers pumped out the water, lifted 900 tonnes of black mud and spread it on fields to dry. Then they planted reeds along one side and built a small bed of sand and gravel where the house pipe ends.

The first refill failed, and the water was green again in three weeks, because the farms were still washing bags. The village argued with the farmers for two meetings before anyone would pay for a washing point. In the end the village paid 12,000 yuan for a concrete washing point with a drain, well away from the pond.

By September the water was clear enough to see the bottom step from the bank. Carp came back, and the village put a bench and a light on the north side. Mr Ou, who has lived beside the pond for forty years, still would not swim in it, but now sits there.

title: The Laundry That Saved Its Last Rinse
paragraphs: A laundry in Tianhe that washes sheets for eleven hotels cut its water use by nearly a third this spring. It handles about 2,400 sheets and 900 towels a day, and it used 90 tonnes of water a day. The new system brings that down to 64 tonnes a day, with the same number of sheets.

The idea is simple: the water from the last rinse is clean enough to use for the first wash. A tank under the floor holds it, and a filter takes out soap and small threads before a pump sends it back. The system cost 150,000 yuan to buy and fit, and took nine days of work.

The first week did not go well, and the worst of it was the filter. The filter blocked twice a day, and 300 sheets came out with grey marks along the folds. One hotel sent back 80 sheets and asked for clean ones by the weekend, so the laundry ran two night shifts.

The owner, Mr Cai, said the marks came from soap that had not been rinsed from the tank. "We were saving water and storing the dirt along with it," Mr Cai said later. A second filter and a short rinse of the tank each morning fixed the problem, at another 9,000 yuan.

The laundry now reuses about 28 percent of its water and saves 7,000 yuan a month on the bill. Mr Cai expects the system to pay for itself in two years, if the price of water holds. He has not bought a bigger tank, because the floor is old and the weight would be too much.

title: The Playground That Drank the Rain
paragraphs: In March, a middle school in Yuexiu replaced 620 square metres of concrete with permeable bricks and a shallow garden. The work cost 210,000 yuan and was meant to stop water standing at the gate after storms. The first heavy rain came on 5 April, and the water stood at the gate anyway.

The bricks worked, and water went through them into a layer of stones below the path. After the rain stopped, the path itself was dry within ten minutes, which surprised the builder. The problem was the garden beside the gate, which filled in twenty minutes and sent water back onto the path.

The reason was a mistake of twelve centimetres, made when the pipe was laid in March. The pipe that lets water into the garden sits higher than the garden, so nothing drains until the path is flooded. The builder, Mr Deng, said the level was checked on a drawing, not on the ground.

Fixing it meant cutting out four metres of pipe and lowering the inlet, at a cost of 6,000 yuan. The gate was closed for two days, so students came in through the side door by the office. The breakfast cart moved to the car park, and Mr Deng's company paid the 6,000 yuan itself.

After the repair, the deepest puddle on the path lasted four minutes instead of forty. A grade 8 class now measures it after every storm and writes the time on a chart in the corridor. The chart shows the garden filling first and the path staying dry, which is the right order.

title: The Skimmer That Broke on the Third Day
paragraphs: In May, a district in Liwan bought a small boat that scoops rubbish from the surface of a river. The boat cost 320,000 yuan and can lift 1.8 tonnes a day with two workers. It replaced four people who had cleaned the same stretch with long nets from the bank.

The boat worked well for two days, and then the river sent it a waterlogged log. The log went under the front belt and jammed it, and two steel teeth broke before the engine stopped. The boat was pulled to the bank and stayed there for five days while a new belt came.

The repair cost 9,000 yuan, and the company said the belt was designed for bottles and leaves. The team leader, Ms Kuang, said the river after heavy rain carries branches, and sometimes furniture. "Nobody told the river what the boat was for," she said, standing beside the empty belt.

The boat also cannot work in shallow water, which is a problem on this stretch. About 400 metres of the river is less than 60 centimetres deep, and the boat needs 70. So two workers with long nets still clean that part by hand, and their work moved to the shallow end.

Since July the boat has worked the deep channel only and collected 41 tonnes, mostly plastic and water plants. A grill now sits in front of the belt to stop logs, and the driver lifts it every hour to look. Ms Kuang still sends one person along the bank to watch for wood before the boat starts.

title: Fifty Blades and One Broken Mould
paragraphs: For thirty-one years, a paper-cutting workshop in Foshan pressed its Spring Festival designs with one steel mould. In January the mould cracked along the edge of a fish pattern, six weeks before the busiest month. A new mould would cost 26,000 yuan and take six weeks to make, which was too long.

The mould was not a simple tool, and its 340 small blades were each bent by hand. It could cut 500 sheets at a time, and 60 percent of the workshop's 40,000 pieces used that pattern. The owner, Ms Su, said no photograph of the blades was clear enough to copy.

A factory in Dongguan made a replacement in five weeks, but the new blades were not the same. They cut two millimetres off one corner, and 3,000 pieces came out with a white line across the fish tail. The workshop sold those pieces at the gate for ten yuan each, and most went in two days.

The person who saved the season was a retired cutter, Ms He, who is seventy-one years old. She redrew the pattern from memory on thin paper, then cut it with a small knife over four days. Her drawing was used to make a second mould, which arrived at the workshop on 2 February.

The workshop finished 31,000 pieces before the festival, about 9,000 fewer than it had planned. Ms Su now keeps two moulds for every main pattern, and a paper copy in a flat box. "A mould is a machine and machines break, but paper does not if the room is dry," she said.

title: Nine Students in the Embroidery Room
paragraphs: An embroidery class in Shunde began in 2019 with twenty-four students, all of them from the town. This spring it has nine students, and they are between sixteen and nineteen years old. The room on the second floor is quiet enough to hear the needles go through the silk.

A piece the size of a hand takes about three months and sells for 4,000 yuan. The silk and the frame cost 800 yuan, and the class keeps the rest for tools and rent. That leaves 3,200 yuan for three months of work, before the shop takes its share.

Two students left in March for a job in a phone shop, where the pay is 4,500 yuan a month. The work there is easier to explain to parents, and it comes with a fixed wage. "I cannot tell a family to wait three months for a sale," the teacher, Ms He, said.

The class has tried two things, and one of them was to move lessons to weekday evenings. Students can now work in the day, and the class also makes small pieces, a flower or a bird. Those sell for 300 yuan and take four days, and six of the nine students make them in their own time.

In May a hotel in the city centre ordered thirty small pieces for its rooms. The order kept the class busy for six weeks, and it paid for the silk for the rest of the year. Ms He says the order helps, but two of the nine still have not said whether they will stay.

title: The Lion Head That Cost More Than a New One
paragraphs: The lion head in a village hall in Panyu is forty-two years old and has danced at every Spring Festival since 1984. In February a dancer fell on it during a practice, and the bamboo frame inside broke in two places. The village then had to decide whether to repair the head or buy a new one.

A workshop quoted 18,000 yuan to rebuild the frame and replace the paper skin, which has 1,200 layers. A new head of the same size costs 9,000 yuan and can be ready in a month. The old head, the workshop said, would never be as strong as it was in 1984.

The village split over the choice, and two long meetings ended without a single vote. Older members wanted the old head repaired, because it was bought with money collected door to door. Younger dancers wanted a new one, lighter by four kilograms, which would let them jump higher.

The compromise took a month, and Mr Luo, who leads the team, said both sides got half. The village paid 11,000 yuan to repair the frame, and kept the old paper skin with its cracks. It also bought a new head for practice, on the condition that it is never used on the festival day.

The old head danced again on the first day of the new year, with the crack above its left eye. The new head is used on Wednesday nights, when the team practises its jumps in the hall. It has already been dropped twice, and nobody in the village seems to mind at all.

title: The Blue That Came Out Grey
paragraphs: In April, a dye workshop in Liwan lost 60 metres of cotton cloth in one batch. The cloth was meant to be deep indigo, the colour of the old work coats, but it came out grey. The batch was worth 7,800 yuan, and it was the workshop's largest order of the spring.

Indigo does not dissolve in water, so the bath needs lime and a powder that takes oxygen out. The dyer, Mr Liang, keeps the bath at about 30 degrees and dips each piece eight times over three days. The cloth comes out green, and it turns blue in the air within a few minutes.

That week the workshop ran out of the powder and bought a box from a new supplier. The box said the same thing, but the powder was weaker and the bath turned warm. Mr Liang added more, and the cloth stopped turning blue, but he did not find out until the sixth dip.

The workshop dipped the cloth again, but the colour washed out in the first rinse. "I trusted the box and did not test the spoon, and in this room one spoon decides the colour," Mr Liang said. He said the mistake was his, and the workshop did not charge the customer for the cloth.

The workshop bought a pH meter for 260 yuan and a notebook for the dye room. It now writes down every spoon, the temperature and the time, and the next 40 metres came out right. Mr Liang says it is still not the same blue as the coats from 1990, and he does not know why.

title: The Workshop With No One Under Thirty
paragraphs: A bamboo weaving workshop in a village near Conghua has seven workers, and the youngest is fifty-four. The average age is sixty-one, and they make baskets for farms and markets at about forty a day. Last autumn they took an order for 3,000 baskets, and by December they had finished 1,800.

The workshop advertised for two months, in the village and at the bus stop on the main road. Four people came to look, and one stayed ten days before he went back to the factory. The pay is 3,600 yuan a month, and a factory in the town pays 5,000 for easier work.

Mr Deng, who is sixty-eight and has woven since he was twelve, said the young ones are not lazy. "They do not see the point of a basket that takes an hour, when a plastic box costs eight yuan," he said. The workshop has stopped taking orders it cannot finish, which the seven workers call sensible.

The village then asked a nearby school to run a six-week class on Friday afternoons. Twenty-two students tried splitting bamboo, and most of them found it harder than it looks. Three signed up for a summer course, and one of them, a girl of fifteen, now comes on Saturdays.

She is fast with the thin strips but slow with the frame, and Mr Deng says that is normal. The workshop has not promised her a job, and she has not asked for one. It has, however, raised its price by ten percent, which the seven workers say is the first good news in years.

title: The Kiln That Was Ten Degrees Too Hot
paragraphs: In March, a pottery workshop in Shiwan fired 120 clay figurines in a single kiln. When the door opened, 41 of them had cracked along the legs, where the clay is thin. The figures were a set of farm animals for a hotel, ordered for the middle of April.

The kiln's thermometer said 1,180 degrees at the top of the firing, which the potter believed. A second gauge, borrowed from a school workshop, said the real heat was 1,290 degrees. The thermometer had not been checked since 2022, so every firing had been hotter than the potter thought.

The workshop's owner, Ms Feng, said the loss was about 6,000 yuan in clay and work. The hotel agreed to wait three weeks, but it asked for a lower price on the second set. The workshop had used the same kiln and the same clay for nine years, and nobody had questioned either.

The next firing used a new thermometer, 900 yuan, and a test piece shaped like a thumb. It came out whole, so the kiln was loaded the next morning with the second set of animals. Ms Feng also slowed the last hour, from 80 degrees an hour to 40, as the old potters did by eye.

The 120 figures were delivered on 18 April, and the hotel paid 4,000 yuan less than the first price. The 41 cracked animals were not thrown away, because a teacher had asked about them. They were sold at the workshop gate for thirty yuan each, and she bought nine for her classroom.

title: Two Hundred Fans and One Wet Summer
paragraphs: A workshop near Zengcheng makes palm-leaf fans, the kind older people use on a hot evening. It sells about 200 a summer at sixty yuan each, and an electric fan costs 120 yuan and lasts five years. The workshop has seven workers, and the youngest of them is fifty-six years old now.

The leaves are cut in October, boiled, bleached in the sun for nine days and pressed flat. A fan takes four days and needs a frame of thin bamboo, which is split by hand. In July the workshop found 70 finished fans with grey-green mould along the edge, after three weeks of rain.

Mould cannot be washed off a palm leaf, so the workers wiped each fan with a dry cloth. Two days in the sun left pale marks on 22 of them, and those were sold at twenty yuan. The rest went back into boxes with a small bag of drying powder that costs four yuan.

Ms Zhou, who is sixty-four and has made fans for forty years, said this was the wettest summer. "A fan is a dry thing, and it lives in the hand, not in a box," she said. "A box in this weather is a small garden," she added, and the workshop lost about 2,900 yuan.

In August it bought a dehumidifier for 2,400 yuan, and the store room now holds 300 fans. The humidity stays at about 55 percent, which is what a dried palm leaf needs. A tea house ordered forty fans to hang on its wall, and they are the first fans nobody will use.

title: Seven Puppets That Would Not Dry
paragraphs: A shadow puppet workshop in Luogang makes its figures from donkey hide, which is scraped thin. The hide must dry in the shade for three days, and each skin takes four days of work. In June a wet week stopped the drying, and seven of the twelve skins went bad.

The workshop tried to hurry, and it put three skins near a heater to dry them. The edges curled like dry leaves, so those three were lost as well, and the workshop stopped. "You see water on the skin and you think of fire, but the skin thinks of its own shape," Mr Wu said.

The lost skins cost about 2,000 yuan, but the order they belonged to was worth much more. A cultural centre had ordered six sets for a spring show, at 2,800 yuan a set, for 20 June. The workshop delivered four sets and asked for two more weeks on the other two.

The centre agreed, on condition that the two sets came with a short talk for school groups. Mr Wu said yes, then spent a week learning what to say and when to stop. The talk is now twelve minutes long, and it begins with a piece of hide, not a finished puppet.

In July the workshop built a drying room for 5,000 yuan, with a fan and two gauges. Skins now dry in four days, whatever the weather, and none have been lost since. Mr Wu has raised his price to 3,100 yuan a set, and the centre has ordered four more.

title: The Silver That Turned Black in a Week
paragraphs: In February, a silver workshop in Liwan made 40 bracelets from a new batch of alloy. Within a week, twelve came back black, and the shops that sold them asked why. The alloy held more copper than the supplier's sheet promised, and the copper had reacted with the air.

The owner, Ms Yan, used to test each batch the way her father taught her, with a drop of liquid. The drop turns dark red when copper is present, and she had never seen it in her shop. She had not tested the new batch, because the supplier had sent the same sheet for eleven years.

Taking back twelve bracelets cost 9,000 yuan, and two of the three shops stopped ordering. The supplier said the batch had been mixed at another factory and offered to replace it. Ms Yan refused the replacement and asked for her money back instead, which took three weeks.

She spent 400 yuan on a testing kit and now tests every batch before it is cut. The test takes twenty minutes and one gram of metal, and she writes the result in a book. The workshop has gone back to its old supplier, whose price has risen by eight percent since 2023.

The bracelets that came back were melted down, and eleven of the twelve are now in the shops. The twelfth had a name cut into it, so the workshop made a new one for that customer. Ms Yan keeps the blackened piece in a drawer by the door, where the light can reach it.

title: Sixty Umbrellas That Would Not Open
paragraphs: A workshop in a town near Huadu has made oil-paper umbrellas by hand since 1978. In April it finished 60 that would not open, because the bamboo ribs split at the fold. The ribs had been cut from young stems that still held water, and the fault showed only at the end.

Each umbrella has 32 ribs, a bamboo handle, a paper skin and three coats of tung oil. It takes six days of work and sells for 85 yuan, and the oil alone costs nine. The workshop buys bamboo from one grower, who cuts stems at least four years old and dries them for six months.

That spring the grower's field was damaged by wind, so the workshop bought 300 stems from another seller. The stems looked the same, but they were two years younger and still held water inside. Nine umbrellas tore when the workers tried to open them, and the other 51 stayed shut.

Mr Huang, who has made umbrellas for thirty-one years, said the fault appeared only after the oil. "Young bamboo is soft, and the oil makes it stiffer than it can bear," he said. The workshop replaced 1,920 ribs and lost three weeks of work before the order was ready.

The museum shop waited and took 20 umbrellas in May, at the old price of 85 yuan. The workshop now writes the year the bamboo was cut on the inside of each handle. It also keeps 200 dry stems, so the next mistake will cost a day rather than a month.

title: The Tap That Filled a Bucket Overnight
paragraphs: On 12 March, a grade 8 class at a middle school in Tianhe put a plastic bucket under a leaking tap in the toilet block and left it there for a full day. In the morning the bucket held 4.6 litres, enough for nine large bottles.

The class had walked past that tap for months, and nobody thought a slow drip mattered, because the sound was soft and the water vanished into the drain. Their teacher, Ms Qiu, asked them to measure it instead of arguing about a repair.

They counted 41 drops in one minute, which works out at 4.6 litres a day and about 138 litres in a month. A check of the whole building then found nine taps dripping in the same way, two of them in the staff room.

The repair took one afternoon and cost 280 yuan for new washers, paid from a fund for small repairs. The school had delayed it because the water bill comes once a term and nobody looks at a single tap. "We were not careless," said the caretaker, Mr Kong. "We just never had a number."

In April the class measured again and found the nine taps had been losing about 1,240 litres a month, close to what a small family uses. The figure is now written above each tap, with one line under it: one drip, one bucket a day.

In June the school added a line to the monthly cleaning list: check every tap on the first Monday. New students still ask about the card, and Ms Qiu lets the class explain the bucket, the drops and the 138 litres themselves.

title: Four Degrees Between Two Classrooms
paragraphs: For one week in November, two grade 8 classes at a school in Yuexiu hung thermometers at the same height and read them three times a day. By Friday one room was 3.9 degrees warmer than the other, and neither class believed it at first.

The rooms hold almost the same number of students, 46 and 45, and they share a wall, so both classes expected the readings to match. The difference turned out to be the windows: one room has a wall of glass facing west.

The gap was clearest at three in the afternoon, when the sun reached the glass. On sunny days the warm room hit 29.6 degrees while the other stayed at 25.7, and on cloudy days the gap fell to 0.8 degrees.

The class took the numbers to the school office and asked for blinds, and the first answer was no, because 2,300 yuan was not in the year's plan. A parent at a factory that makes blinds offered the material, so the school paid only for fittings.

The blinds went up in the first week of December, and a second week of readings showed the gap at 1.1 degrees on sunny afternoons. Students in the warm room also stopped opening the door to cool it, which had made the corridor cold.

"We stopped guessing," said their teacher, Ms Xia. "The thermometer did the talking, and the office listened to it faster than it listened to us." The class now lends the thermometers to other rooms and keeps a small chart in the corridor.

title: Forty-Seven Kilograms in One Bin
paragraphs: In the last week of September, students at a middle school in Panyu weighed every plate left on the tables in the canteen. They used two kitchen scales and one notebook, and the total for five days came to 236 kilograms of food.

About 600 students eat lunch at the school, so the waste worked out at 47 kilograms a day, or roughly 80 grams per student. Over a 200-day school year that is more than nine tonnes, enough to fill a small truck twice over.

The students then looked inside the bins on three separate days and wrote down what they saw. Rice made up about half the weight, whole buns came next, and many students said the rice portion was simply too large for them to finish.

In November the canteen tried smaller rice bowls and let students ask for a second bowl for free. Waste fell by 22 percent in three weeks, the bowls cost about 1,600 yuan, and the kitchen saved more than that in rice before the term ended.

Not everyone was pleased with the change. Some older students said the small bowls made lunch feel like a test, and a few took two bowls and left the second one on the table. The group still weighs every Friday, rain or shine.

The next step is a table by the door where students can leave unopened buns for anyone who wants one. The canteen has agreed to try it for two weeks in April, with a sign and one member of the group standing beside it.

title: Seventy-One Degrees on the Roof of a Bus
paragraphs: On a July afternoon, six students from a school in Baiyun stood at a bus stop with an infrared thermometer and measured the roof of a parked bus. The metal read 71 degrees, while the air around them was 34.

They had borrowed the thermometer from the physics lab and spent two weeks learning how to use it properly. The plan was to compare four surfaces in the same sun: the bus roof, the asphalt road, a metal bench and the grass in a small park.

The results were uneven: asphalt reached 63 degrees, the bench 58, and the grass stayed at 33. The bus roof was hottest because it is dark and flat, and because the air under it cannot move, so the seats inside were 46 degrees.

The students sent a one-page report to the bus company. An engineer wrote back to say the company had already tried white paint on two buses. That lowered the roof by about 9 degrees, but the paint peeled off after four months.

In September the company painted three more roofs and agreed to park buses in shade where possible. The students now measure the roofs once a month and add each new number to the report, which the engineer says he keeps on his desk.

The six students also measured their own classroom roof, which read 64 degrees and has no shade at all. The school is considering a light-coloured cover for one section, but the cost of about 8,000 yuan has not been approved.
